   \mathbf1_{rl\in\mathcal L\mathcal R}|F(l)|^2|G_1(r)|^2\right]
 \le-N+C_1Nm^{-\varepsilon}+C(n+m).$$

Also $\log[ |S_N|/(|\mathcal L||\mathcal R|)]\le N+O(\log N)$ by applying the upper bound $\log(N!)\le N\log N-N+O(\log N)$ to the numerator and the lower bounds $\log(m!)\ge m\log m-m$, $\log(n!)\ge n\log n-n$ to the denominator. This one-sided bound is all the recursion needs. This proves <a href="#tra:tilted-arrays:eq6" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:tilted-arrays:eq6">[tra:tilted-arrays:eq6]</a>, taking a sufficiently small fixed positive $\eta$ (e.g. less than $\varepsilon/3$ and $1/4$), for all sufficiently large $d$. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-32"></a>
#### Unordered bad rows at sparse levels

The weak regular moment controls representations of large dimension. The remaining input is an operator bound when the first row is long. We first cancel isolated paths, then estimate the mean of the resulting absolute kernel, and finally control exceptional input rows in every output column.

<a id="stmt-tra-tilted-arrays-sparse-statement"></a>
<div id="tra:tilted-arrays:sparse-statement" class="lemma">

<a id="tra:tilted-arrays:eq10"></a>
**Lemma 31**. *<span id="tra:tilted-arrays:sparse" label="tra:tilted-arrays:sparse"></span> Fix $0<\delta<1$. We need the following bound: if $\lambda_1=N-k$ where $1\le k\le N^{1-\delta}$, then the operator norm in this representation of $T_N$ is at most $$N^{-b k} \label{tra:tilted-arrays:eq10}$$ for some $b=b(\delta)>0$ and $d$ sufficiently large. On the sign twist it is even zero (this latter statement also holds for $k=0$).*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-tra-tilted-arrays-sparse-statement"><summary>Proof of stmt-tra-tilted-arrays-sparse-statement</summary>

*Proof.* <span id="tra:tilted-arrays:sparse-proof" label="tra:tilted-arrays:sparse-proof"></span> <span id="tra:tilted-arrays:forest-and-unordered-set-proof" label="tra:tilted-arrays:forest-and-unordered-set-proof"></span> To prove this, let $\mathcal X$ be ordered $k$-tuples of distinct positions, measure $\nu$ uniform on $\mathcal X$. Functions on $\mathcal X$ are acted on by position permutations. The shape $\lambda$ occurs here and does not occur in functions of any proper subset of the coordinates. Indeed occurrence on $k$-tuples is having invariants under $S_{N-k}$, by the action on tuples and its stabilizer, and the branching rule says this holds for shapes with first row at least $N-k$. Smaller coordinate subsets would require a larger first row.

For $S\subseteq [k]$, put $s=|S|$, and for $x,y\in\mathcal X$ let $$R_S(x,y)=N^s\,\mathbb P(g(x_S)=y_S),$$ using the pass permutation. The full $R_{[k]}$ as an integral kernel against $\nu$ represents $T_N^*$ on tuple functions (the forward transition kernel is the adjoint under our action convention), up to the factor $N^k/(N)_k$. Also, in bilinear forms on a copy of $\lambda$, the proper subset terms give zero since they only involve those subsets of coordinates. Thus we can bound the desired norm by giving an operator norm bound on $$Z_*(x,y)=\sum_{S\subseteq [k]}(-1)^{k-|S|}R_S(x,y) .$$

A path of a card from one address to another in the $d$-layer pass is unique: at each coordinate it must go to the bit given by its destination address. It occurs with probability $1/N$; it is prescribed by individual switch choices. Make a graph on $[k]$ using $x,y$, putting an edge whenever the two associated paths use the same switch at some layer (in the same or different directions, including use of the same switch input). If there is an isolated vertex, $Z_*=0$. In fact such a path then imposes switch choices independent of those for any other subset of paths, which gives cancellation in pairs due to the scaling by $N$. Writing $\Gamma$ for the event the graph has no isolated vertex, define $$W(x)=\int\sum_S R_S(x,y)\mathbf 1_\Gamma\,d\nu(y),$$ an upper bound on the absolute row integral. We have $W(x)\le e^{Ck}$, since the row integral of each $R_S$ is $N^s/(N)_s\le e^s$. Likewise $e^{Ck}$ bounds columns using the inverse pass. We will obtain much smaller bounds by controlling typical rows and showing their exceptions cannot concentrate in any column.

<a id="tra:tilted-arrays:eq11"></a>
First, for some $\gamma=\gamma(\delta)>0$, $$\mathbf E_\nu W\le N^{-\gamma k}. \label{tra:tilted-arrays:eq11}$$ For $k=1$ the no-isolated-vertex event is impossible, so take $k\ge 2$. In bounding each average over $x,y$, we can take all $x_i,y_i$ iid addresses and relax distinctness at cost at most $e^{2k}$, using the same $R_S$ definition also on repeats. Weighting that iid law by $R_S$ gives a simple sampling rule: sample a full pass network, take all $x_i$ iid, use $y_i=g(x_i)$ on $S$, and sample the other $y_i$ iid. Conditional on this network the resulting single-card paths are independent. At each layer the switch used by each such path is uniform among $N/2$ switches: on $S$ this is by uniform start through the fixed network, and outside $S$ by iid start and finish (the address along the path uses respective bits of these). Therefore for any forest on the cards with $u$ edges, the probability its edges are all path interactions is at most $(2d/N)^u$: for a leaf relative to its parent path this bound per edge follows by union over layers, and leaves can be peeled off using independence conditional on network. If $\Gamma$ holds, there is a forest with $u$ between $k/2$ and $k-1$ edges. At each such size there are at most $(C k)^u$ to try, by choosing edges. Hence we have upper bound $$2^k e^{2k}\sum_{\lceil k/2\rceil\le u\le k-1}(C k d/N)^u$$ for <a href="#tra:tilted-arrays:eq11" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:tilted-arrays:eq11">[tra:tilted-arrays:eq11]</a>, proving the claim for the indicated range of $k$.

The mean estimate alone does not control a matrix norm: a small collection of input rows might carry a large operator. The next domination estimate rules this out in each fixed output column.

<a id="tra:tilted-arrays:eq12"></a>
Next, for any set $\mathcal B$ of $x$’s depending only on the unordered set of their entries, we have, for every fixed $y\in\mathcal X$, $$\int_{\mathcal B} R_S(x,y)\,d\nu(x)\le e^{Ck}\nu(\mathcal B). \label{tra:tilted-arrays:eq12}$$ To see it we can again use iid $x$ at cost at most $e^k$, asking also for distinctness along with $\mathcal B$. Weighting by $R_S$ amounts here to setting $x_S=g^{-1}(y_S)$ and sampling remaining $x_i$ iid. Under this inverse network, the set occupied by the $s$ paths satisfies, for each set of sites $T$ at any stage, probability of containing $T$ at most product over $T$ of the current site marginals. Indeed this property holds initially for the deterministic set at $y_S$, and remains true through each fair random transposition, which suffices as these give the layers. For $T$ using one of the switched sites, average the previous bounds with that site exchanged, and for using both, use that product of the two site marginals is bounded by product after averaging the two; other marginals have not changed. At the end the site marginals are $s/N$ by the uniform single-position transition. Thus probability for the set of $s$ sites to equal any particular $s$-set is at most $(s/N)^s$, interpreted as 1 for $s=0$. For all of $x$ to have as entries a given $k$-set, distinctly, in this law, probability is thus at most $$\binom{k}{s}(s/N)^s (k-s)!/N^{k-s}
 \le e^k k!/N^k .$$ The probability for that set under $\nu$ is $k!/(N)_k$, giving <a href="#tra:tilted-arrays:eq12" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:tilted-arrays:eq12">[tra:tilted-arrays:eq12]</a> as desired.

Now $W(x)$ is unordered-set measurable by simultaneous reindexing of $x,y$, so the rows with $W>N^{-\gamma k/2}$ make a bad set of the kind in <a href="#tra:tilted-arrays:eq12" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:tilted-arrays:eq12">[tra:tilted-arrays:eq12]</a>, having $\nu$-probability at most $N^{-\gamma k/2}$. For $Z_*$ restricted to good rows, its absolute row and column integrals are at most $N^{-\gamma k/2}, e^{Ck}$, respectively; on bad rows, bounds $e^{Ck},e^{C'k} N^{-\gamma k/2}$ apply respectively by <a href="#tra:tilted-arrays:eq12" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:tilted-arrays:eq12">[tra:tilted-arrays:eq12]</a> and $|Z_*|\le \sum_S R_S$. Schur’s operator norm bound (square root of product of row and column bounds) proves <a href="#tra:tilted-arrays:eq10" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:tilted-arrays:eq10">[tra:tilted-arrays:eq10]</a>, decreasing positive constants in exponents as needed. Here in passing to the copy of $\lambda$ we indeed multiply the integral kernel by at most 1 to account for the earlier factor $N^k/(N)_k$.

Finally if we twist the tuple representation by sign, for $k<N/2$ averaging even one network layer already gives the zero operator. For each tuple there is a switched pair fixing all its positions (i.e. using two unoccupied positions), so the signed subgroup average there cancels. This proves the sign twist claim. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-33"></a>
#### A bounded recursive exponent

<a id="stmt-tra-tilted-arrays-main-statement"></a>
<div id="tra:tilted-arrays:main-statement" class="theorem">

<a id="tra:tilted-arrays:eq1"></a>
**Theorem 32**. *<span id="tra:tilted-arrays:moment" label="tra:tilted-arrays:moment"></span> There is a sequence $r(d)\ge2$ with $\sup_d r(d)<\infty$ such that $$\mathcal Z_N(r(d))\le 6/5
\qquad(d\ge1). \label{tra:tilted-arrays:eq1}$$ For every deterministic initial deck and every integer $w\ge\sup_d r(d)$, the law after $wd$ physical shuffles has chi-square divergence at most $1/5$ from uniform, and hence total-variation distance at most $\frac12\sqrt{1/5}$ from uniform.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-tra-tilted-arrays-main-statement"><summary>Proof of stmt-tra-tilted-arrays-main-statement</summary>

*Proof of Theorem <a href="#tra:tilted-arrays:moment" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="tra:tilted-arrays:moment">[tra:tilted-arrays:moment]</a>.* <span id="tra:tilted-arrays:moment-induction" label="tra:tilted-arrays:moment-induction"></span> The weak moment and the sparse operator bound are independent inputs. We now show that they cover every representation and that the exponent increases at successive splits have a bounded product.

<a id="tra:tilted-arrays:eq13"></a>
<a id="tra:tilted-arrays:eq14"></a>
We spell out which representations are covered by <a href="#tra:tilted-arrays:eq10" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:tilted-arrays:eq10">[tra:tilted-arrays:eq10]</a> and its sign version, taking $\delta=\eta/4$ for the $\eta$ in <a href="#tra:tilted-arrays:eq6" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:tilted-arrays:eq6">[tra:tilted-arrays:eq6]</a>. Write $D_\lambda$ for dimensions. For large $d$, unless $$\log D_\lambda\ \ge\ N^{1-\eta/2}, \label{tra:tilted-arrays:eq13}$$ we necessarily have $$k=N-\max(\lambda_1,\lambda^{\mathsf t}_1)\ \le\ N^{1-\delta}. \label{tra:tilted-arrays:eq14}$$ Here is one way to check. Put $h=\max(\lambda_1,\lambda^{\mathsf t}_1)$, and if $h\le N/10$, the hook-length formula already gives at least $(5/e)^N$ from hooks at most $2h$. Else we can transpose if needed and take $h$ as the first row length. If there are at least $z=\lfloor N^{1-\delta}\rfloor$ boxes below the row, take a subdiagram consisting of the row and just $z$ such boxes. The dimension of the original is at least the number of standard fillings of this subdiagram, which is at least $\binom{h}{z}$. In fact one can fill the first $z$ boxes of the top row first (having $z<h$), then freely interleave its remainder with the lower part in a fixed standard order on that part, since all lower boxes are in columns at most $z$; and fillings extend to the original. This suffices for <a href="#tra:tilted-arrays:eq13" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:tilted-arrays:eq13">[tra:tilted-arrays:eq13]</a>, proving <a href="#tra:tilted-arrays:eq14" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:tilted-arrays:eq14">[tra:tilted-arrays:eq14]</a> when <a href="#tra:tilted-arrays:eq13" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:tilted-arrays:eq13">[tra:tilted-arrays:eq13]</a> fails.

Choose a fixed $r_{\min}\ge2$ with $2br_{\min}\ge4$, where $b$ is the sparse constant for $\delta=\eta/4$. At each level $k$ in <a href="#tra:tilted-arrays:eq14" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:tilted-arrays:eq14">[tra:tilted-arrays:eq14]</a> there are at most $2^{k+1}$ shapes, allowing transpose, and each has dimension at most $N^k$. The sign twists are annihilated by the sparse lemma; for the other nonconstant shapes, <a href="#tra:tilted-arrays:eq10" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:tilted-arrays:eq10">[tra:tilted-arrays:eq10]</a> bounds their regular contribution at every $u\ge r_{\min}$ by $$\sum_{1\le k\le N^{1-\delta}}
       2^{k+1}N^{2k-2bku}=o(1).$$ The sign representation itself also contributes zero. These are the first class in Lemma <a href="#lem:balanced-moment-closure" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:balanced-moment-closure">19</a>, with $\varepsilon=1/5$; their contribution is at most $1/10$ above an absolute threshold.

The remaining class satisfies <a href="#tra:tilted-arrays:eq13" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:tilted-arrays:eq13">[tra:tilted-arrays:eq13]</a>. Use the positive-square convention $\nu=2$ and set $$E_N=N^{1-\eta},\qquad H_N=N^{1-\eta/2},\qquad
 \alpha_d=2-\alpha,\qquad\delta_d=d^{-1/2}.$$ Proposition <a href="#tra:tilted-arrays:recursion" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="tra:tilted-arrays:recursion">[tra:tilted-arrays:recursion]</a> supplies its child-to-parent hypothesis uniformly for inherited exponents at least $r_{\min}$. The decisive comparison is $$(1+\delta_d)E_N-\delta_dH_N
 =(1+d^{-1/2})N^{1-\eta}-d^{-1/2}N^{1-\eta/2}
 \longrightarrow-\infty.$$ Also $(2-\alpha)(1+d^{-1/2})=1+O(d^{-1/2})$. The common lemma therefore supplies bounded recursive exponents $r(d)$ satisfying <a href="#tra:tilted-arrays:eq1" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:tilted-arrays:eq1">[tra:tilted-arrays:eq1]</a>, including the finite initial sizes. <span id="tra:tilted-arrays:fourier-completion" label="tra:tilted-arrays:fourier-completion"></span> Its positive-square convention means the matching singular exponent is $2\sup_d r(d)$. Proposition <a href="#e:nonnormal-moment-conversion" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="e:nonnormal-moment-conversion">16</a> gives chi-square divergence at most $1/5$ after every integer $w\ge\sup_d r(d)$ of forward sweeps, uniformly over initial decks. Since each sweep is $d$ physical shuffles, the stated total-variation bound follows. ◻

</details>

<a id="tra:fractional-density"></a>
### Fractional densities and a harmonic infinity bound

This section gives an alternative proof of the balanced compatibility bound using fractional integrability and a softened survival potential. Theorem <a href="#tra:duality:weighted" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="tra:duality:weighted">[tra:duality:weighted]</a> already implies the compatibility estimate below for sufficiently large sizes. The proof here obtains its coefficient integrability by spectral bins, without inverse Hausdorff–Young, and carries that bound through the entropy exposure. Its separate sparse result is an infinity-norm estimate on harmonic tuples, with an explicit constant and the full range $k\le n/(2d)$.

One sweep is $d$ physical shuffles. All regular traces are unnormalized. We use $T_n$ and $Q_n=T_n^*T_n$ as in Section <a href="#sec:prelim" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:prelim">2</a>.

<a id="tra:fractional-density:eq1"></a>
<span id="tra:fractional-density:density-normalization" label="tra:fractional-density:density-normalization"></span> We will use the left regular representation of $S_n$. For a finite group $G$ in general, write $\mathcal L(g)$ for the left regular operators. We identify group algebra elements with operators in this representation, calling $f$ the density of $Z$ if $$Z=\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g\in G} f(g)\mathcal L(g)$$ (where $f$ need not be a probability density). With ordinary, *unnormalized* trace, we have $$f(g)=\operatorname{Tr}\mathcal L(g^{-1})Z,\qquad
 \mathbb E_{g\ \mathrm{unif.}} |f(g)|^2=\operatorname{Tr}(Z^*Z).
 \label{tra:fractional-density:eq1}$$ For $S_n$, let $\Pi_i$ be the average operator for the random swap layer at bit $i$. This is an orthogonal projection, since it averages over the subgroup generated by all the disjoint transpositions in the layer. Set $$T_n=\Pi_d\cdots\Pi_1,\qquad Q_n=T_n^* T_n,\qquad
 M_n(p)=\operatorname{Tr}(Q_n^p)\quad (p>0).$$ We have $0\le Q_n\le I$, and $M_n(p)\ge 1$ by the constants. We use the notation $T_n,Q_n,M_n$ also with other powers of two as the size (using that size’s own scan).

<span id="tra:fractional-density:power-log-majorization-and-mixing" label="tra:fractional-density:power-log-majorization-and-mixing"></span> For later comparison, a positive integer $L$ satisfies <a id="tra:fractional-density:eq3"></a>$$n!\sum_g \Pr(g\ \text{is the movement in }L\ \text{scans})^2
  =\operatorname{Tr}\big((T_n^L)^*T_n^L\big)\ \le\ M_n(L).
 \label{tra:fractional-density:eq3}$$ The inequality is Schatten Hölder, as used in Proposition <a href="#e:nonnormal-moment-conversion" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="e:nonnormal-moment-conversion">16</a>. A positive-square moment of order $p$ is a singular moment of order $2p$, so $M_n(p)\le1+1/8$ supplies Proposition <a href="#e:nonnormal-moment-conversion" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="e:nonnormal-moment-conversion">16</a> with singular exponent $2p$ and remainder $1/8$.

<a id="tra:fractional-density:eq4"></a>
The positive-power comparison, Lemma <a href="#lem:positive-power-comparison" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:positive-power-comparison">9</a>, with $P=4r$ and $q=4$, also gives the form used below: $$\operatorname{Tr}(B^{1/2}AB^{1/2})^{2r}
 \le\operatorname{Tr}(A^rB^rA^rB^r)
 \qquad(A,B\ge0,\ r\ge1).
 \label{tra:fractional-density:eq4}$$

<a id="tra:fractional-density:induction-budgets"></a>
#### The induction step and rough moment

All logarithms in the proof below are natural logs. Fix the constants $$\alpha=\frac{1}{64},\qquad \beta=\frac{1}{256},\qquad c_0=\frac18,$$ and let $$a=2^{\lceil d/2\rceil},\qquad b=2^{\lfloor d/2\rfloor},\qquad
 n=ab,\qquad \delta=d^{-1/2}.$$

<a id="stmt-tra-fractional-density-step-and-rough-moment"></a>
<div id="tra:fractional-density:step-and-rough-moment" class="proposition">

**Proposition 33**. *<span id="tra:fractional-density:step" label="tra:fractional-density:step"></span>*

<a id="tra:fractional-density:eq5"></a>
<a id="tra:fractional-density:eq6"></a>
<a id="tra:fractional-density:eq7"></a>
*For all sufficiently large $d$, if a real $q\ge16/\beta$ satisfies $$M_b(q), M_a(q) \ \le\ 1+c_0,
 \label{tra:fractional-density:eq5}$$ then $p_0=(1+\delta)q$ satisfies $$M_n((1+\delta)p_0)\le 1+c_0
 \label{tra:fractional-density:eq6}$$ and $$M_n(p_0)\le \exp(n^{1-\alpha}).
 \label{tra:fractional-density:eq7}$$ The lower threshold for $d$ is absolute and independent of $q$.*

</div>

We first prove the rough estimate <a href="#tra:fractional-density:eq7" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:fractional-density:eq7">[tra:fractional-density:eq7]</a> by splitting the array. Its sublinear exponent will control the large-dimensional representations in <a href="#tra:fractional-density:eq6" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:fractional-density:eq6">[tra:fractional-density:eq6]</a>; small levels will be bounded directly on tuples of positions.

<span id="tra:fractional-density:balanced-operator-split" label="tra:fractional-density:balanced-operator-split"></span> **Rough bound via a balanced split.** View positions as an $[a]$-by-$[b]$ array with row index made from the last $\lceil d/2\rceil$ bits and column index from the first $\lfloor d/2\rfloor$ bits (using $[m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}$). The scan first operates by horizontal permutations in $$H=(S_b)^a$$ and then by vertical permutations in $$V=(S_a)^b$$ where these are the subgroups preserving each row and each column, respectively. In fact the first part of the scan just does independent size-$b$ scans, one in each row, and then the second part does independent size-$a$ scans, one in each column. Write the average operators of those two parts as $K_H,K_V$, so $T_n=K_V K_H$. Set $$A=K_H K_H^*,\qquad B=K_V^* K_V,\qquad r=p_0/2.$$ Since $Q_n=K_H^* B K_H$, it has the same eigenvalues as $B^{1/2} A B^{1/2}$. Thus <a href="#tra:fractional-density:eq4" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:fractional-density:eq4">[tra:fractional-density:eq4]</a> gives <a id="tra:fractional-density:eq8"></a>$$M_n(p_0)\le \operatorname{Tr}(A^r B^r A^r B^r).
 \label{tra:fractional-density:eq8}$$

<span id="tra:fractional-density:coefficient-probability-reduction" label="tra:fractional-density:coefficient-probability-reduction"></span> The line factors of $A^r$ and $B^r$ are $(T_bT_b^*)^r$ and $(T_a^*T_a)^r$, respectively. Let their coefficient densities be $f_R,f_D$. Their squared masses are $M_b(p_0),M_a(p_0)$, both in $[1,2]$ by <a href="#tra:fractional-density:eq5" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:fractional-density:eq5">[tra:fractional-density:eq5]</a> and $p_0\ge q$.

<a id="tra:fractional-density:eq10"></a>
For $h=(h_i)\in H$ and $v=(v_j)\in V$, the entropy exposure uses arrays $$X_{ij}=h_i(j)\in[b],\qquad Y_{ij}=v_j^{-1}(i)\in[a],
 \qquad
 \mathcal E=\{(X_{ij},Y_{ij})\text{ are all distinct}\}.$$ This is the domain $hv\in VH$ in the proof of Lemma <a href="#lem:coefficient-compatibility" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:coefficient-compatibility">14</a>: at the intermediate cell $(i,j)$, after $v$ and before $h$, the input row is $Y_{ij}$ and the output column is $X_{ij}$. Opposite-order routing is possible exactly when each input row sends one card to each output column. Define the product probability law $\nu$ on these arrays by the independent line densities $$\rho_R(x)=\frac{|f_R(x)|^2}{M_b(p_0)},\qquad
 \rho_D(y)=\frac{|f_D(y^{-1})|^2}{M_a(p_0)}.$$ The same lemma, using the equivalent $hv\in VH$ form of its four-factor calculation, gives $$M_n(p_0)\le\frac{n!}{|H||V|}
      M_b(p_0)^a M_a(p_0)^b\,\nu(\mathcal E).
 \label{tra:fractional-density:eq10}$$ We estimate the last probability, keeping the estimate robust under the density changes in $\nu$.

<a id="tra:fractional-density:eq11"></a>
<span id="tra:fractional-density:fractional-spectral-density" label="tra:fractional-density:fractional-spectral-density"></span> First consider a single row or column law $\nu_*$ in this product, on $S_m$ with $m=b$ or $a$. For the row case let $T=(T_m T_m^*)^q$; for the column case let $T=(T_m^* T_m)^q$. By hypothesis $0\le T\le I$ and $\operatorname{Tr} T\le 2$ in the regular representation for this $m$. We deal with the density of $F=T^{(1+\delta)/2}$, evaluated on permutations for the row case and on their inverses for the column case. Divide the positive eigenvalues of $T$ into intervals $$(e^{-l-1},e^{-l}]\qquad (l=0,1,\ldots),$$ and correspondingly write $F=\sum_l F_l$ using spectral parts (only finitely many nonzero). Then $$\operatorname{Tr} F_l\le 2 e^{(1-\delta)(l+1)/2},
 \qquad
 \operatorname{Tr} F_l^2\le 2 e^{-\delta l}.$$ Write $f_l$ for the associated density (evaluated on inverses in the column case). By <a href="#tra:fractional-density:eq1" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:fractional-density:eq1">[tra:fractional-density:eq1]</a>, $$\|f_l\|_\infty\le \operatorname{Tr} F_l\le 2e^{(l+1)/2},\qquad
 \|f_l\|_2^2\le 2e^{-\delta l},$$ where the first inequality follows because $F_l$ is positive semidefinite and the $\mathcal L(g)$ are unitary. Norms for functions here are with uniform measure. Thus $$\|f_l\|_{2+\delta}^{2+\delta}
 \le C e^{-\delta l/2}$$ for an absolute $C$, taking $d$ large so $0<\delta\le 1$. Adding the norms gives $$\left\|\sum_l f_l\right\|_{2+\delta}\le C'/\delta$$ by summing a geometric series, with $C'$ absolute. Therefore the density $\rho$ of $\nu_*$, which equals the square modulus of $\sum_l f_l$ divided by a number at least 1, satisfies $$\mathbb E_{U_m}\rho^{1+\delta/2}\le (C'/\delta)^{2+\delta}
 \label{tra:fractional-density:eq11}$$ where $U_m$ denotes uniform on $S_m$.

<a id="tra:fractional-density:eq12"></a>
<a id="tra:fractional-density:eq13"></a>
<span id="tra:fractional-density:density-relative-entropy-comparison" label="tra:fractional-density:density-relative-entropy-comparison"></span> We use relative entropy $D(P\|R)=\mathbb E_P\log(P/R)$ for probability laws, infinite if $P$ is not supported on the support of $R$. From <a href="#tra:fractional-density:eq11" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:fractional-density:eq11">[tra:fractional-density:eq11]</a>, with $$\epsilon=\frac{\delta}{2+\delta},$$ any law $\mu$ on $S_m$ satisfies $$D(\mu\|\nu_*)\ \ge\ \epsilon D(\mu\|U_m)-O(\log d).
 \label{tra:fractional-density:eq12}$$ In fact we use the elementary variational inequality $$D(P\|R)\ \ge\ \mathbb E_P W-\log \mathbb E_R e^W
 \label{tra:fractional-density:eq13}$$ for potentials $W$ (also allowing $-\infty$ on points outside the support of $P$ with the exponential expectation positive). This follows by changing the reference measure by the exponential tilt and using nonnegativity of relative entropy. In <a href="#tra:fractional-density:eq12" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:fractional-density:eq12">[tra:fractional-density:eq12]</a>, assuming finite divergence, apply <a href="#tra:fractional-density:eq13" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:fractional-density:eq13">[tra:fractional-density:eq13]</a> with $P=\mu$, $R=U_m$, and $W=(1+\delta/2)\log\rho$, and use $D(\mu\|\nu_*)=D(\mu\|U_m)-\mathbb E_\mu\log\rho$. This gives <a href="#tra:fractional-density:eq12" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:fractional-density:eq12">[tra:fractional-density:eq12]</a> because of <a href="#tra:fractional-density:eq11" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:fractional-density:eq11">[tra:fractional-density:eq11]</a> and $\delta=d^{-1/2}$.

<a id="stmt-tra-fractional-density-compatibility-probability"></a>
<div id="tra:fractional-density:compatibility-probability" class="lemma">

**Lemma 34**. *<span id="tra:fractional-density:compatibility" label="tra:fractional-density:compatibility"></span>*

<a id="tra:fractional-density:eq14"></a>
*The compatibility probability satisfies $$\nu(\mathcal E)
 \ \le\ \exp\left(-n+O\left(n a^{-1/16}\log a+(a+b)\log d\right)\right).
 \label{tra:fractional-density:eq14}$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-tra-fractional-density-compatibility-probability"><summary>Proof of stmt-tra-fractional-density-compatibility-probability</summary>

*Proof.* <span id="tra:fractional-density:compatibility-proof" label="tra:fractional-density:compatibility-proof"></span>

<a id="tra:fractional-density:eq15"></a>
<span id="tra:fractional-density:entropy-decomposition-and-reveal" label="tra:fractional-density:entropy-decomposition-and-reveal"></span> Consider any law $\zeta$ on arrays supported on $\mathcal E$, assuming $D(\zeta\|\nu)<\infty$. Write $X_i=X_{i,\cdot}$ for the row permutations and $Y_j=Y_{\cdot,j}$ for the column permutations (using single subscripts for these permutations). We use $\zeta_X,\zeta_{X_i},\zeta_{Y_j}$, etc., for the laws of parts of the arrays under $\zeta$. Put $$D_X=D(\zeta_X\|U_b^{\otimes a}),\qquad
 D_Y=\sum_{j\in[b]}D(\zeta_{Y_j}\|U_a),\qquad
 J=\mathbb E_{X\sim\zeta_X}D\Big(\zeta_{Y\mid X}\ \Big\|\ \bigotimes_{j\in[b]}\zeta_{Y_j}\Big).$$ By <a href="#tra:fractional-density:eq12" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:fractional-density:eq12">[tra:fractional-density:eq12]</a>, $$D(\zeta\|\nu)
 \ \ge\ J+\epsilon(D_X+D_Y)-O((a+b)\log d).
 \label{tra:fractional-density:eq15}$$ Indeed, decomposing the joint divergence against the product law $\nu$, we get $J$, plus $D(\zeta_X\| \bigotimes_i \nu_{X_i})$, plus the divergences of the $\zeta_{Y_j}$ against their individual laws in $\nu$. For the $X$ term, decompose further into $D(\zeta_X\| \bigotimes_i\zeta_{X_i})$ and the sum of individual marginal divergences. Applying <a href="#tra:fractional-density:eq12" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:fractional-density:eq12">[tra:fractional-density:eq12]</a> to the individual divergences and keeping at least an $\epsilon$ fraction of $D(\zeta_X\| \bigotimes_i\zeta_{X_i})\ge 0$ gives <a href="#tra:fractional-density:eq15" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:fractional-density:eq15">[tra:fractional-density:eq15]</a>.

To lower bound $J$, consider drawing the arrays from $\zeta$, with $X$ revealed first. Take independent uniform priorities $t_j\in[0,1]$, independent also of the arrays, and expose $Y$ column by column, in order of *decreasing* $t_j$. Within each column reveal its entries in increasing order of $i$. For any fixed priorities (ignoring null events of ties), the chain formula for relative entropy gives $J$ as a sum of expected conditional divergences, one per cell $(i,j)$. In that cell the divergence is between:

- the conditional distribution of $Y_{ij}$ under $\zeta$, given $X$, earlier columns, and earlier entries in column $j$;

- the law $u$ with

$$u_y=\zeta_{Y_j}(Y_{ij}=y\mid Y_{1j},\ldots,Y_{i-1,j}),\qquad y\in[a].$$ The second (reference) law depends just on previous entries in the *same* column. Though we suppress its cell and history indices on $u,u_y$, we always take conditionals at histories arising under $\zeta$. Since we know $X$, the first distribution is supported on candidates that are not *blocked*, where $y$ is blocked if $(X_{ij},y)$ has already occurred as a pair in an earlier column.

Put $$g(j,x)=|\{i': X_{i'j}=x\}|.$$ Call the cell bad if $g(j,X_{ij})>a^{1/8}$, good otherwise. Call a candidate $y$ high if $u_y>a^{-1/4}$, low otherwise. Let $R_X$ count bad cells, and $R_Y$ cells whose actual $Y_{ij}$ is high. These counts depend on the outcome arrays (and law $\zeta$ for defining high), but not the priorities.

<span id="tra:fractional-density:low-candidate-potential" label="tra:fractional-density:low-candidate-potential"></span> For a good cell in the chain formula, apply <a href="#tra:fractional-density:eq13" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:fractional-density:eq13">[tra:fractional-density:eq13]</a> to the conditional divergence, using $\eta=a^{-1/16}$ and this potential: $$W(y)=
 \begin{cases}
 0, & y\ \text{high},\\
 -\infty, & y\ \text{low and blocked},\\
 -\log(t_j+\eta), & y\ \text{low and not blocked}.
 \end{cases}$$ On bad cells just take $W(y)=0$. These choices depend only on what is given before the cell, besides the priorities and the law. The actual choice under $\zeta$ is not blocked and has $u_y>0$ almost surely, so the reference normalization in <a href="#tra:fractional-density:eq13" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:fractional-density:eq13">[tra:fractional-density:eq13]</a> is positive as needed.

For the log normalization term of <a href="#tra:fractional-density:eq13" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:fractional-density:eq13">[tra:fractional-density:eq13]</a>, condition now on the entire outcome arrays $(X,Y)$ and on $t_j$, and average over the other priorities. Assume the cell is good and write $x=X_{ij}$. For each $y$, including each low candidate, the pair $(x,y)$ occurs exactly once in the outcome arrays, since $\mathcal E$ holds and there are $ab$ cells. If its occurrence is in another column, the probability the candidate is not blocked is $t_j$, since the priority of that column is uniform independent. The candidates occurring in the current column with $x$ number at most $g(j,x)$, so the total $u$ mass of those among them which are low is at most $a^{1/8} a^{-1/4}$. Writing $Z=\sum_y u_y e^{W(y)}$, this gives $$\mathbb E\big[ Z\mid X,Y,t_j\big]
 \ \le\ \sum_{y\ \mathrm{high}} u_y
       +\frac{t_j}{t_j+\eta}\sum_{y\ \mathrm{low}} u_y
       +\frac{a^{1/8}a^{-1/4}}{\eta}
 \ \le\ 1+a^{-1/16}.$$ This computation uses that $u$ is fixed in this conditioning, as the within-column order is fixed. On a bad cell $Z=1$. We get in particular $\mathbb E\log Z\le a^{-1/16}$ by Jensen’s inequality.

<a id="tra:fractional-density:eq16"></a>
For the expected-potential term in <a href="#tra:fractional-density:eq13" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:fractional-density:eq13">[tra:fractional-density:eq13]</a>, averaging over histories under $\zeta$ amounts to using the actual score $W(Y_{ij})$. For each good cell whose actual choice is low, since good/low status for the actual choice is independent of the priorities, its score with the priorities averaged is $$\int_0^1 -\log(t+\eta)\,dt
 =1-(1+\eta)\log(1+\eta)+\eta\log\eta
 =1-O(a^{-1/16}\log a),$$ and it is 0 on the other cells. The displayed integral lies between 0 and 1 for sufficiently large $a$. Since the chain formula for $J$ holds for each fixed priority vector with distinct entries, averaging our lower bounds over priorities and summing all cells gives $$J\ \ge\ n-\mathbb E_\zeta[R_X+R_Y]-O(n a^{-1/16}\log a).
 \label{tra:fractional-density:eq16}$$

<a id="tra:fractional-density:eq17"></a>
<a id="tra:fractional-density:eq18"></a>
<span id="tra:fractional-density:high-atom-and-clump-charge" label="tra:fractional-density:high-atom-and-clump-charge"></span> The counts lost in <a href="#tra:fractional-density:eq16" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:fractional-density:eq16">[tra:fractional-density:eq16]</a> can be paid for by the deficits $D_X,D_Y$. First, for $D_Y$, use its chain formula for the marginal column laws against uniform permutations, within each column in increasing $i$. While the number remaining to be revealed in the column (including the current cell) is at least $\sqrt a$, the high subset has uniform conditional probability at most $a^{-1/4}$, since it has size at most $a^{1/4}$. Use <a href="#tra:fractional-density:eq13" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:fractional-density:eq13">[tra:fractional-density:eq13]</a> with potential $(\log a)/8$ on the high subset and 0 outside, to see that the conditional divergence at this cell, from $u$ against the uniform choice among those remaining, is at least $$\frac{\log a}{8}\sum_{y\ \mathrm{high}} u_y - a^{-1/8}.$$ Skipping fewer than $\sqrt a$ cells at the end of each column (their conditional divergences are nonnegative), taking marginal expectations, and summing gives $$D_Y\ \ge\ \frac{\log a}{8}\big(\mathbb E_\zeta R_Y - n a^{-1/2}\big)-n a^{-1/8}.
 \label{tra:fractional-density:eq17}$$ For $D_X$, we claim for large $a$, $$D_X\ \ge\ \frac{\log a}{16}\mathbb E_\zeta R_X-1.
 \label{tra:fractional-density:eq18}$$ To verify this let $\gamma=(\log a)/16$ and $h_0=a^{1/8}$. Under $U_b^{\otimes a}$, the reference law for $D_X$, the probability of any specification of $z$ different cells to prescribed values in $X$ is at most $(e/b)^z$. For a compatible specification this follows row by row because for $z_i$ cells in one row its probability is $1/(b(b-1)\cdots(b-z_i+1))$, at most $(e/b)^{z_i}$ by $b!\ge (b/e)^b$ (the geometric mean in the descending product for the row is at least that from $b!$). Incompatible specifications have probability zero. Also, $$e^{\gamma R_X}
  =\prod_{j,x\in[b]}
       \left(1+\big(e^{\gamma g(j,x)}-1\big)\mathbf 1_{\{g(j,x)>h_0\}}\right).$$ To bound its expectation, expand this product. For each selected $(j,x)$ with $g(j,x)=s>h_0$, bound by specifying $s$ rows having $X_{ij}=x$, summing over the choices and using factor $e^{\gamma s}$ (for the probability bound we do not need to require that there are no further matching entries). In a term with several selected $(j,x)$, if the specifications conflict they have probability zero, and otherwise they require distinct cells. Thus $$\mathbb E_{U_b^{\otimes a}} e^{\gamma R_X}
 \le \left(1+\sum_{s>h_0}\binom{a}{s} (a^{1/16} e/b)^s\right)^{b^2}
 \le e$$ for all sufficiently large $a$. Indeed the sum inside is at most $\sum_{a\ge s>h_0} (2 e^2 a^{1/16}/s)^s$ using $a/b\le 2$; this goes to zero faster than any inverse power of $a$. Applying <a href="#tra:fractional-density:eq13" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:fractional-density:eq13">[tra:fractional-density:eq13]</a> proves <a href="#tra:fractional-density:eq18" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:fractional-density:eq18">[tra:fractional-density:eq18]</a>.

Since $\epsilon\log a$ tends to infinity, <a href="#tra:fractional-density:eq17" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:fractional-density:eq17">[tra:fractional-density:eq17]</a>-<a href="#tra:fractional-density:eq18" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:fractional-density:eq18">[tra:fractional-density:eq18]</a> in <a href="#tra:fractional-density:eq15" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:fractional-density:eq15">[tra:fractional-density:eq15]</a> absorb the terms $\mathbb E_\zeta[R_X+R_Y]$ from <a href="#tra:fractional-density:eq16" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:fractional-density:eq16">[tra:fractional-density:eq16]</a>. We conclude $$D(\zeta\|\nu)
 \ \ge\ n-O\left(n a^{-1/16}\log a+(a+b)\log d\right).$$ Taking $\zeta=\nu(\cdot\mid\mathcal E)$ when $\nu(\mathcal E)>0$, this proves <a href="#tra:fractional-density:eq14" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:fractional-density:eq14">[tra:fractional-density:eq14]</a>. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-36"></a>
###### Completion of the rough moment estimate.

Stirling’s formula gives $$\log\frac{n!}{|H||V|}
 =\log n!-a\log(b!)-b\log(a!)
 = n + O((a+b)\log n).$$ Hence <a href="#tra:fractional-density:eq10" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:fractional-density:eq10">[tra:fractional-density:eq10]</a>, <a href="#tra:fractional-density:eq14" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:fractional-density:eq14">[tra:fractional-density:eq14]</a>, and $M_b(p_0),M_a(p_0)\le 2$ bound $M_n(p_0)$ by the exponential of at most $O(n^{31/32}\log n)$, using $a,b=\Theta(\sqrt{n})$. This proves <a href="#tra:fractional-density:eq7" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:fractional-density:eq7">[tra:fractional-density:eq7]</a> for all sufficiently large $d$.

<a id="pm-h-37"></a>
#### An infinity estimate on harmonic tuples

<a id="stmt-tra-fractional-density-harmonic-infinity-statement"></a>
<div id="tra:fractional-density:harmonic-infinity-statement" class="proposition">

**Proposition 35**. *<span id="tra:fractional-density:harmonic" label="tra:fractional-density:harmonic"></span><span id="e:harmonic-smoothing" label="e:harmonic-smoothing"></span>*

<a id="tra:fractional-density:eq19"></a>
*Let $n=2^d$ with $d\ge1$, let $T_n$ be one coordinate sweep, and put $Q_n=T_n^*T_n$. Take $1\le k\le n/(2d)$ and consider the representation on functions on ordered injective $k$-tuples of positions, with $g\in S_n$ acting by $$(\pi_k(g)F)(v)=F(g^{-1}v)$$ where the notation on $v$ acts on all its positions. Write $\pi_k$ also for the corresponding action of group algebra elements. Call a function harmonic here if the sum in any one coordinate with the others fixed is 0 (taking the sum over the remaining available positions for that coordinate). The space of these functions is invariant under the permutation actions. We claim an infinity norm bound on this space: $$\|\pi_k(Q_n) F\|_\infty
 \ \le\ \left(\frac{C_* d k}{n}\right)^{k/2}\|F\|_\infty
 \qquad(F\ \text{harmonic})
 \label{tra:fractional-density:eq19}$$ with $C_*=2(4e)^2$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-tra-fractional-density-harmonic-infinity-statement"><summary>Proof of stmt-tra-fractional-density-harmonic-infinity-statement</summary>

*Proof.* <span id="tra:fractional-density:harmonic-proof" label="tra:fractional-density:harmonic-proof"></span>

<a id="tra:fractional-density:eq20"></a>
<span id="tra:fractional-density:midpoint-occupation-and-signed-path-laws" label="tra:fractional-density:midpoint-occupation-and-signed-path-laws"></span> In fact $(\pi_k(Q_n)F)(v)$ is the expectation of $F$ on the tuple after moving $v$ through a scan and then an independent reverse scan (layers in reverse order). This follows from $Q_n=T_n^*T_n$ and the representation action. Start the tuple at $v$ and let its ordered midpoint tuple between the scans be $w$. For any set $D$ of $k$ positions, we have $$\Pr(\{w_1,\ldots,w_k\}=D)\le (k/n)^k .
 \label{tra:fractional-density:eq20}$$ To see this, during the first scan consider just the occupied set of the $k$ labels. At any point its law, with occupancy marginal probabilities $p_x$ on positions, satisfies the bound $\Pr(D'\ \text{all occupied})\le\prod_{x\in D'}p_x$ for any subset $D'$. This holds initially, and is preserved through any one independent fair pair swap: the marginals of the two positions are replaced by their average. For a subset containing exactly one of these positions, averaging the two previous bounds gives the new bound; for a subset containing both, the probability stays the same and the product bound can only increase; for subsets containing neither there is no change. We can apply this through the sequence of all individual swaps. At the midpoint each card separately is uniform on the positions, since in its path each bit has been randomized with a fresh fair choice. Therefore $p_x=k/n$ for the occupancy marginals, giving <a href="#tra:fractional-density:eq20" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:fractional-density:eq20">[tra:fractional-density:eq20]</a>.

Condition on $w$. Index the $k$ labels in the tuple by $[k]$. For $S\subseteq[k]$, consider a law $\mathcal P_{S,w}$ of $k$ paths in the second (reverse) scan with the following dynamics:

- the labels in $S$ follow a common reverse scan with its random switches;

- every other label (omitted from $S$) just follows a path using its own independent choices to stay or swap in the scheduled bit at each stage.

<a id="tra:fractional-density:eq21"></a>
We allow the path positions under these laws not to form injective tuples across all the labels; extend $F$ by 0 on noninjective tuples. For $S\ne[k]$, the expectation of $F$ at the endpoint under $\mathcal P_{S,w}$ is 0. Indeed any omitted label has a uniform final position independent of the others. If the other final positions are distinct we use harmonicity and the extension by 0, and if not, $F$ is already 0. Thus applying the signed sum of path laws $$\sum_{S\subseteq[k]} (-1)^{k-|S|}\mathcal P_{S,w}
 \label{tra:fractional-density:eq21}$$ to $F$ at the endpoint gives the same expectation as the true second scan.

<span id="tra:fractional-density:isolated-cancellation-and-rooted-forest-count" label="tra:fractional-density:isolated-cancellation-and-rooted-forest-count"></span> For any tuple of paths in these laws consider its encounter graph on $[k]$, joining two labels if they enter the same switch in some stage (possibly at the same position). The signed sum <a href="#tra:fractional-density:eq21" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:fractional-density:eq21">[tra:fractional-density:eq21]</a> vanishes on any path tuple whose encounter graph has an isolated vertex. In fact if a vertex is isolated, toggling it in or out of $S$ doesn’t change the path tuple probability. To realize fixed paths in the common switches just requires the corresponding values of the switch coins, with probability zero in case of conflict. The isolated path uses $d$ switches disjoint from those of any other paths (indexing switches by stage as well as pair), so it imposes its values independently, with probability $2^{-d}$, just as if using its own omitted-label choices. This proves the cancellation.

<a id="tra:fractional-density:eq22"></a>
Consequently the absolute conditional endpoint expectation in the true second scan is at most $\|F\|_\infty G(w)$, where $$G(w)=\sum_{S\subseteq[k]}\mathcal P_{S,w}(\text{encounter graph has no isolated vertex}).$$ The function $G(w)$ is symmetric under reordering $w$: all choices of $S$ are summed and the dynamics and condition correspond under renaming labels. Therefore <a href="#tra:fractional-density:eq20" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:fractional-density:eq20">[tra:fractional-density:eq20]</a> gives $$\mathbb E G(w)\le \frac{(k/n)^k}{k!}\sum_{w\ \text{injective ordered}} G(w).
 \label{tra:fractional-density:eq22}$$

To bound the last sum, fix $S$ and fix its entire set of common switch coins and the separate stay/swap choice coins for omitted labels, using the same coins simultaneously for any starting $w$. For each individual label, the map from its own starting position to its position entering any given stage is then a permutation of the $n$ positions. This is true for a label in $S$ by the common switch layers; for any other label the fixed choices apply bit flips or not, also giving permutations. For these coins, count the starting $w$’s whose encounter graph has no isolated vertex. Each such graph contains a spanning forest with $c\le k/2$ components each of size at least 2; take a root in each component. (If $k=1$ there are no such graphs.) For given $c$, the number of rooted forests involved is at most $\binom{k}{c} k^{k-c}$, by choosing roots and parents. For a fixed forest, the starting positions of its roots can be chosen in at most $n^c$ ways. For every other vertex, once the parent’s starting position has been chosen, there are at most $2d$ choices, since at some stage the child’s path must enter the switch that the parent enters. At a given stage there are at most two choices of the child’s starting position by the permutation property. Hence the number of $w$’s satisfying all the encounters of this forest is at most $n^c(2d)^{k-c}$, not even needing to enforce injectivity in this bound. Using this count and averaging over coins for each $S$, <a href="#tra:fractional-density:eq22" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:fractional-density:eq22">[tra:fractional-density:eq22]</a> implies $$\begin{aligned}
 \mathbb E G(w)
 &\le \frac{(k/n)^k}{k!}\,2^k
  \sum_{1\le c\le k/2} \binom{k}{c} (2d k)^{k-c} n^c\\
 &\le (2e)^k \sum_{1\le c\le k/2} \binom{k}{c} (2d k/n)^{k-c}
 \ \le\ \left(\frac{C_* d k}{n}\right)^{k/2}.
 \end{aligned}$$ In the last inequality we used $2dk/n\le 1$ and can take $C_*=2(4e)^2$. This establishes <a href="#tra:fractional-density:eq19" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:fractional-density:eq19">[tra:fractional-density:eq19]</a>. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-e-harmonic-singular-conversion"></a>
<div id="e:harmonic-singular-conversion" class="corollary">

**Corollary 36** (Singular values at a first-row level). *Let $\lambda\vdash n$ have first row $n-k$, where $1\le k\le n/(2d)$. Then $$\|Q_n(\lambda)\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \le \left(\frac{2(4e)^2dk}{n}\right)^{k/2},
 \qquad
 \|T_n(\lambda)\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \le \left(\frac{2(4e)^2dk}{n}\right)^{k/4}.$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-e-harmonic-singular-conversion"><summary>Proof of stmt-e-harmonic-singular-conversion</summary>

*Proof.* The ordered $k$-tuple module is induced from the trivial representation of $S_{n-k}$. Branching and Frobenius reciprocity show that $V_\lambda$ occurs in it, by removing the $k$ boxes below the first row. It does not occur in any $(k-1)$-tuple module: every diagram there has first row at least $n-k+1$. The span of functions lifted by omitting one coordinate therefore has no $\lambda$-isotypic component. Its orthogonal complement is exactly the harmonic space, because orthogonality to every such lift means that each coordinate sum vanishes.

The operator $Q_n(\lambda)$ is positive. Every eigenvector in a copy of $V_\lambda$ inside the harmonic space satisfies the infinity-norm bound of Proposition <a href="#e:harmonic-smoothing" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="e:harmonic-smoothing">[e:harmonic-smoothing]</a>; dividing by its nonzero infinity norm bounds its eigenvalue. This proves the first inequality. The second follows from $Q_n(\lambda)=T_n(\lambda)^*T_n(\lambda)$. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-38"></a>
#### Closing the trace recursion

<details id="proof-stmt-e-harmonic-singular-conversion-2"><summary>Proof of stmt-e-harmonic-singular-conversion</summary>

<a id="tra:fractional-density:eq24"></a>
*Proof of Proposition <a href="#tra:fractional-density:step" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="tra:fractional-density:step">[tra:fractional-density:step]</a>.* <span id="tra:fractional-density:sparse-irrep-transfer" label="tra:fractional-density:sparse-irrep-transfer"></span> Put $s=\lfloor n^{1-\beta}\rfloor$. For large $d$, $s<n/(2d)$, so Corollary <a href="#e:harmonic-singular-conversion" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="e:harmonic-singular-conversion">36</a> applies to all first-row levels $1\le k\le s$. Its positive-eigenvalue bound is <a id="tra:fractional-density:eq23"></a>$$(C_*dk/n)^{k/2}\le n^{-\beta k/4},
 \label{tra:fractional-density:eq23}$$ since $k/n\le n^{-\beta}$. There are at most $2^k$ shapes of level $k$, each of dimension $r_\lambda\le n^k$. Thus their complete regular contribution at any $p\ge16/\beta$ is at most $$\sum_{1\le k\le s}2^kn^{2k-p\beta k/4}=o(1).
 \label{tra:fractional-density:eq24}$$ This uses the bound at the smallest allowed $p$, so the size threshold is uniform over the inherited exponent.

<span id="tra:fractional-density:sign-annihilation-and-catalan-dimensions" label="tra:fractional-density:sign-annihilation-and-catalan-dimensions"></span> A matching layer annihilates every shape with more than $n/2$ rows, as in the proof of Theorem <a href="#tra:duality:moment" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="tra:duality:moment">2</a>. In particular all shapes with $n-\lambda'_1\le s$ vanish, since $n-s>n/2$ for sufficiently large $n$.

<a id="tra:fractional-density:eq25"></a>
Treat the one-row shape separately: it is the trivial representation and contributes 1 to $M_n(p)$. All shapes not handled so far have $$n-\lambda_1>s,\qquad n-\lambda'_1>s.$$ For them we have $$r_\lambda\ge \exp(c s)
 \label{tra:fractional-density:eq25}$$ for some absolute $c>0$ when $d$ is sufficiently large. For if $\lambda_1\ge s$, we can find a subdiagram consisting of a first row of length $s$ and $s$ more boxes below it forming a tail partition (as there are at least $s$ boxes available below, taking a subpartition of size $s$, of width necessarily at most $s$). The number of standard tableaux of this subdiagram is at least the Catalan number $\frac{1}{s+1}\binom{2s}{s}$. Indeed interleave filling the top row and filling the $s$-box tail in the order of any fixed standard tableau on the tail, keeping the number of filled top row boxes always at least the number of filled tail boxes. This ballot condition ensures any tail box being filled already has the required top-row box above in its column (the column index is at most the number reached in filling the tail). Each resulting tableau extends to the original shape by filling the rest after the subdiagram. This proves <a href="#tra:fractional-density:eq25" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:fractional-density:eq25">[tra:fractional-density:eq25]</a> in the case considered; the case $\lambda'_1\ge s$ follows as well by transposing. If both lengths are smaller than $s$, then every hook length is at most $2s$, so $$r_\lambda\ge n!/(2s)^n,$$ which also gives <a href="#tra:fractional-density:eq25" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:fractional-density:eq25">[tra:fractional-density:eq25]</a> for large enough $d$, since $n/(2s)$ tends to infinity.

<span id="tra:fractional-density:large-dimension-trace-attenuation" label="tra:fractional-density:large-dimension-trace-attenuation"></span> Apply the one-step estimate of Lemma <a href="#lem:balanced-moment-closure" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:balanced-moment-closure">19</a> with the positive-square convention $\nu=2$, remainder $\varepsilon=1/8$, low-level baseline $P=16/\beta$, and $$E_n=n^{1-\alpha},\qquad H_n=cs,\qquad
 \alpha_d=1+d^{-1/2},\qquad\delta_d=d^{-1/2}.$$ Here <a href="#tra:fractional-density:eq7" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:fractional-density:eq7">[tra:fractional-density:eq7]</a> is the rough child-to-parent bound, <a href="#tra:fractional-density:eq24" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:fractional-density:eq24">[tra:fractional-density:eq24]</a> makes the low-level remainder at most $1/16$, and <a href="#tra:fractional-density:eq25" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:fractional-density:eq25">[tra:fractional-density:eq25]</a> provides the regular multiplicity of every remaining block. The large-block remainder is bounded by $$\exp\{(1+d^{-1/2})n^{1-\alpha}
               -c d^{-1/2}\lfloor n^{1-\beta}\rfloor\}=o(1),$$ because $\beta<\alpha$. It is therefore at most $1/16$ above an absolute threshold independent of $q$. Adding the constant contribution proves <a href="#tra:fractional-density:eq6" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:fractional-density:eq6">[tra:fractional-density:eq6]</a>. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-tra-fractional-density-bounded-moment-conclusion"></a>
<div id="tra:fractional-density:bounded-moment-conclusion" class="theorem">

**Theorem 37**. *<span id="tra:fractional-density:moment" label="tra:fractional-density:moment"></span>*

*There are numbers $p(d)>0$, with $\sup_d p(d)<\infty$, such that for every $n=2^d$, <a id="tra:fractional-density:eq2"></a>$$M_n(p(d))\le 1+c_0,\qquad c_0=\frac18.
 \label{tra:fractional-density:eq2}$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-tra-fractional-density-bounded-moment-conclusion"><summary>Proof of stmt-tra-fractional-density-bounded-moment-conclusion</summary>

*Proof of Theorem <a href="#tra:fractional-density:moment" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="tra:fractional-density:moment">[tra:fractional-density:moment]</a>.* <span id="tra:fractional-density:finite-base-and-bounded-order" label="tra:fractional-density:finite-base-and-bounded-order"></span> The application of Lemma <a href="#lem:balanced-moment-closure" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:balanced-moment-closure">19</a> just verified has exponent multiplier $(1+d^{-1/2})^2=1+O(d^{-1/2})$. The lemma supplies the common finite base and bounds the product of these multipliers over rounded halvings. It therefore gives the asserted bounded sequence $p(d)$. Proposition <a href="#e:nonnormal-moment-conversion" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="e:nonnormal-moment-conversion">16</a> applies with singular exponent $2\sup_dp(d)$ and remainder $1/8$. ◻

</details>

<a id="tra:asymmetric"></a>
### Asymmetric grids and integrated spectral projections

All the preceding grids have comparable side lengths. We now change the aspect ratio itself. Short cycles in the resulting array and fixed-size coordinate chunks supply estimates adapted to unequal child scales.

A split into a short coordinate block and a long block produces a different trace recursion. Sparse partitions are first controlled by interpolation on an enlarged tuple space, with fixed-size coordinate chunks. For the dense estimate, the associated bipartite graph has few edges belonging to a parallel pair or a four-cycle. Those edges account for the entropy error, and a support cutoff in each spectral integral pays for the number of local partition types.

Write $n=2^e$ in this section, and let $T_n$ be one sweep. Schatten norms are unnormalized, and $d_\lambda$ is the dimension of the irreducible indexed by $\lambda\vdash n$. The operator is a product of subgroup projections and has a strict norm gap off constants at each fixed size by Lemma <a href="#lem:finitegap" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:finitegap">5</a>. <span id="tra:asymmetric:strip-interpolation" label="tra:asymmetric:strip-interpolation"></span> We use the strip interpolation established in the proof of Lemma <a href="#lem:positive-power-comparison" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:positive-power-comparison">9</a>. For a bounded analytic matrix family $F$ on $0\le\Re z\le1$, continuous on the boundary, $$\|F(iu)\|_{\rm op}\le1,\qquad \|F(1+iu)\|_{S^q}\le B
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \|F(\theta)\|_{S^{q/\theta}}^{q/\theta}\le B^q.$$ Below $q$ is $2$ or $4$. Complex powers are zero on their kernels, as in that proof.

<a id="pm-h-40"></a>
#### Fixed-size coordinate chunks on enlarged tuples

<a id="stmt-tra-asymmetric-sparse-statement"></a>
<div id="tra:asymmetric:sparse-statement" class="proposition">

<a id="tra:asymmetric:eq1"></a>
**Proposition 38**. *<span id="tra:asymmetric:sparse" label="tra:asymmetric:sparse"></span> **Long first row.** For all sufficiently large powers of two $n$, if $$1\le k=n-\lambda_1\le n^{.995},$$ there is a bound $$d_\lambda\,{\rm Tr}|T_n(\lambda)|^p\le n^{-10k}
                       \qquad (p\ge p_*)
               \label{tra:asymmetric:eq1}$$ with $p_*<\infty$ absolute.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-tra-asymmetric-sparse-statement"><summary>Proof of stmt-tra-asymmetric-sparse-statement</summary>

*Proof.* <span id="tra:asymmetric:sparse-proof" label="tra:asymmetric:sparse-proof"></span> <span id="tra:asymmetric:macro-coordinate-interpolation" label="tra:asymmetric:macro-coordinate-interpolation"></span> Use the permutation representation on ordered $K$-tuples of distinct positions, where $K=\lfloor k n^{.001}\rfloor$; thus $K/n\le n^{-.004}$. Split the coordinate sequence into chunks of lengths between $\ell$ and $2\ell$, where $\ell$ will just be a sufficiently large *constant*, and $e$ can be taken sufficiently large. So the positions are tuples of macro coordinates, ranging in sets of sizes $L_j$, each between $2^\ell$ and $2^{2\ell}$. A sweep updates these macro coordinates in sequence, doing sweeps $T_{L_j}$ independently in every fibre of coordinate $j$, by which we mean with all other macro coordinates fixed. For the ordered $K$-tuples this means the operator of a chunk is block diagonal, with a block specified by the allocation of tuple members to fibres. On such a block it is a tensor product: for a fibre with $t$ members use $T_{L_j}$ acting on ordered $t$-tuples (using fixed ordering of the members in this factor).

<a id="tra:asymmetric:eq2"></a>
For any such local operator $T$ write $T=V|T|$ with unitary polar factor, and replace it by $$T(z)=V |T|^{Qz/2}.$$ Apply these replacements in every block, and let $F(z)$ be the product of the resulting chunk operators in the sweep order. We can take $Q>2$ a sufficiently large constant depending on $\ell$. On the first line of the strip the operator norms are at most 1. On the second line $T(z)$ is arbitrarily close to the matrix averaging uniformly on its local tuple space, since $T$ preserves constants with all other singular values strictly less than 1 by the generation observation; only finitely many local sizes are used. For $t=0,1$ we have the averaging exactly on this line (a sweep gives a single point all fresh fair bits). In particular we take $Q$ so that on this line, with $L=L_j$, each entry of $T(z)$ in absolute value is at most $$\frac{1+\delta_L(t)}{(L)_t},\qquad
       \delta_L(0)=\delta_L(1)=0,\quad \delta_L(t)=L^{-2}\ (t\ge2),
               \label{tra:asymmetric:eq2}$$ with $(L)_t$ a falling factorial.

<a id="tra:asymmetric:eq3"></a>
Between any given input and output ordered tuple, there is at most one trajectory of tuples through the chunk product: at each boundary of chunks, the already processed macro coordinates of each point must be its output ones and the others its input ones. A valid such trajectory, under *ideal* routing doing full uniform permutations independently in each fibre at each chunk, has probability given by multiplying $1/(L)_t$ for its fibres. Thus <a href="#tra:asymmetric:eq2" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:asymmetric:eq2">[tra:asymmetric:eq2]</a> bounds the sum of squared entries of $F(z)$ by $$(n)_K\ \mathbb E\prod_{\text{fibres over chunks}}
                     \frac{(1+\delta_L(t))^2}{(L)_t}
         \ \le\ \mathbb E\prod_{\text{fibres over chunks}} W_L(t),
         \qquad W_L(t)= (1+\delta_L(t))^2\frac{L^t}{(L)_t}.
                 \label{tra:asymmetric:eq3}$$ Here we sample the starting $K$-tuple uniformly and do the ideal routing, $t$ referring to the occupancy by those routed points; we used $\prod_j L_j=n$.

<a id="tra:asymmetric:eq4"></a>
We detail why clustering of the $K$ points in this estimate is harmless. Condition on the full ideal routing of all $n$ points, let $X$ be the uniform size $K$ sample of input points, and use the graph on $n$ points connecting any two that visit the same fibre at any chunk. Maximum degree is $O_\ell(\log n)$. Consider a component $Y$ of the induced graph on the sample, of size $v$. Over all chunks its fibre occupancies satisfy $$\sum t\log t\le v\log v .
                      \label{tra:asymmetric:eq4}$$ In fact, group the inputs by their not-yet-processed coordinates: form the tree starting with all inputs and splitting by the input coordinate of the last chunk, then the next-to-last, and so on. Take any node specified by coordinates later than $j$, split into children by coordinate $j$. The points of $Y$ here (say of number $v_0>0$) when routed up to chunk $j$ are distributed over fibres still within the specified later coordinates, and the $t$ in one fibre come from $t$ different children because their $j$-coordinates are distinct and not yet processed. Hence the sum of $t\log t$ over these fibres is at most $v_0$ times the entropy of the child proportions: average the distributions over children given by each fibre (each distribution uniform on $t$ children with weight $t/v_0$) and use concavity. Summing the bounds at nodes telescopes, giving <a href="#tra:asymmetric:eq4" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:asymmetric:eq4">[tra:asymmetric:eq4]</a>. There is no shared occupied fibre of two different components.

For $t\ge 2$, $$\log W_L(t)\le \frac{C}{\log L}\,t\log t$$ with $C$ absolute. Up to $\sqrt L$ use $\log(L^t/(L)_t)=O(t^2/L)$; above that, it suffices that this log is at most $t$, using the average over the full increasing sequence $\log(L/(L-i)),\,0\le i<L$. Choose $\ell$ so large that by this and <a href="#tra:asymmetric:eq4" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:asymmetric:eq4">[tra:asymmetric:eq4]</a> the product in <a href="#tra:asymmetric:eq3" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:asymmetric:eq3">[tra:asymmetric:eq3]</a> is bounded by the product over nonsingleton components of $v^{\zeta v}$, $\zeta=.0005$.

With $\Delta=O_\ell(\log n)$ a degree bound (at least 1), and $u=K/n$, the expectation of this last product is at most $$\exp\left(\sum_{v=2}^K n\Delta^{2(v-1)} u^v v^{\zeta v}\right).$$ Indeed we can sum products over collections of disjoint connected sets included in $X$, charging the components in particular; the probability cost for such a collection is at most $u$ to the power of total size. The count of connected sets uses a spanning tree walk of length $2(v-1)$; allowing arbitrary collections with the product cost gives the exponential bound. The sum in this exponential is $O(n\Delta^2 u^2)$: for $v\ge3$ compare after factoring $n\Delta^2 u^2$ to powers of $\Delta^2 u n^{3\zeta}$, which goes to zero. Thus <a href="#tra:asymmetric:eq3" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:asymmetric:eq3">[tra:asymmetric:eq3]</a> is at most $\exp(O(k))$, since $\Delta^2 K^2/n=O(k)$ for our $k,K$.

The enlarged tuple space has now supplied a Schatten budget $\exp(O(k))$. Its large branching multiplicity will convert that budget into decay on each first-row level. We now interpolate. We have $\|F(1+iy)\|_2^2\le\exp(O(k))$, whereas $F(2/Q)$ is the sweep operator on the $K$-tuple space, so its Schatten $Q$-norm to power $Q$ has the same upper bound. By branching and Frobenius reciprocity for the pointwise stabilizer of $K$ positions, the multiplicity of $\lambda$ in this space is the number of standard tableaux of the skew shape obtained by removing the row of length $n-K$ from $\lambda$. Since $\lambda_2\le n-K$ here (for large enough $n$), there are at least $\binom Kk$ such tableaux: the tail of size $k$ is separate from the remaining $K-k$ entries of the first row. The Schatten estimate with this multiplicity thus gives, say, $$\|T_n(\lambda)\|_{\rm op}^Q\le n^{-.0004 k}$$ for all sufficiently large $n$ (use $K/k\ge n^{.001}/2$). As $d_\lambda\le n^k$ (it occurs even on ordered $k$-tuples), increasing to a suitably large constant power $p_*$ proves <a href="#tra:asymmetric:eq1" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:asymmetric:eq1">[tra:asymmetric:eq1]</a>. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-tra-asymmetric-dimension-and-annihilation"></a>
<div id="tra:asymmetric:dimension-and-annihilation" class="lemma">

<a id="tra:asymmetric:eq5"></a>
**Lemma 39**. *<span id="tra:asymmetric:dimension" label="tra:asymmetric:dimension"></span> We record two further partition details. If $\lambda$ has length greater than $n/2$, we have $T_n(\lambda)=0$. Indeed there are no invariants under even one full pair layer subgroup. This also follows immediately in the Specht module realization: the irrep is spanned by column-antisymmetrized vectors (polytabloids) from tableaux, and the column of length greater than $n/2$ must contain both endpoints of some pair, so averaging kills such vectors. For all sufficiently large $n$, for the partitions of length at most $n/2$ with $k>n^{.995}$, we have $$\log d_\lambda\ \ge\ n^{.995}.
                      \label{tra:asymmetric:eq5}$$ In fact if the first row has length $r\ge n/10$, keep a subshape of the diagram with this row and $t=\lfloor n^{.995}/2\rfloor$ boxes below. Even on this shape we get at least $\binom rt$ tableaux: after the first $t$ boxes of the first row are filled we can interleave the rest of that row and a standard filling of the lower boxes. They extend to the whole shape. This count suffices for <a href="#tra:asymmetric:eq5" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:asymmetric:eq5">[tra:asymmetric:eq5]</a>. We can do the same with the first column if it has length at least $n/10$ (there are enough boxes outside the column by the length condition). If neither holds, <a href="#tra:asymmetric:eq5" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:asymmetric:eq5">[tra:asymmetric:eq5]</a> follows by the hook length formula with all hooks at most $n/5$.*

</div>

<a id="tra:asymmetric:grid-sizes"></a>
#### Short-cycle entropy on an asymmetric grid

For the regular-representation part of the proof, take, with $n=2^e$ large, $$a=2^{\lfloor e/10\rfloor},\qquad b=n/a.$$

<a id="stmt-tra-asymmetric-compatibility-statement"></a>
<div id="tra:asymmetric:compatibility-statement" class="proposition">

<a id="tra:asymmetric:eq6"></a>
**Proposition 40**. *<span id="tra:asymmetric:compatibility" label="tra:asymmetric:compatibility"></span> Arrange the points in $b$ rows of $a$ cells each. We need a probability bound, which we prove first. Independently in each row $i$, assign the labels $h_{ij}\in[a]$ by a permutation, with an arbitrary law of density at most $D_i$ relative to uniform. Independently each column $j$ has labels $l_{ij}\in[b]$ likewise assigned by a permutation, say with density at most $D'_j$, also independent across columns and from the row assignments. Put $D_H=\prod_i D_i,\ D_L=\prod_j D'_j$. Then, with an absolute constant $C$, the probability that the pairs $(h_{ij},l_{ij})$ are all distinct is at most $$\exp\left(-n+C n^{.98}
                        +\frac{C}{\log n}\log(D_H D_L)\right).
                     \label{tra:asymmetric:eq6}$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-tra-asymmetric-compatibility-statement"><summary>Proof of stmt-tra-asymmetric-compatibility-statement</summary>

*Proof.* <span id="tra:asymmetric:compatibility-proof" label="tra:asymmetric:compatibility-proof"></span> <span id="tra:asymmetric:short-cycle-and-matching-entropy" label="tra:asymmetric:short-cycle-and-matching-entropy"></span> For the proof, the $l$-array gives a bipartite multigraph on sides of size $b$, with one edge from $i$ to $l_{ij}$ per cell; it has degree $a$. Call an edge bad if contained in a parallel pair or in a 4-cycle. Write $L_{\rm bad}$ for the number of bad edges (cells).

<a id="tra:asymmetric:eq7"></a>
<a id="tra:asymmetric:eq8"></a>
Here is a useful moment bound for these edges under the uniform independent column assignments $\mathcal U$: $$\log\mathbb E_{\mathcal U}\exp(c(\log n)L_{\rm bad})
                                      = O(n^{.9})
                       \label{tra:asymmetric:eq7}$$ for some absolute $c>0$. Compare any law $\xi$ of column assignments to $\mathcal U$ by KL divergence (relative entropy). Use the chain rule revealing one cell at a time in an order given by independent uniform priorities. For a current cell, if at least $b/3$ values are still available in its column, test the event that its new edge closes a parallel pair or a 4-cycle with edges already visible; otherwise use an empty event as test. Under the $\mathcal U$-conditional distribution, chance of the test event is $O(a^3/b)=O(n^{-.6})$; the possible targets from paths of length 1 or 3 are bounded in number by $a+a^3$. Thus each conditional KL divergence is bounded below by $$.25(\log n)\Pr_{\xi}(\text{test event}\mid\text{past})-O(n^{-.35}),$$ where the order is given (use the entropy inequality with $.25\log n$ times the indicator as test function). For a given completed array, each bad edge will score the event with at least absolute positive probability over order. Indeed fix up to three witnessing other edges; with probability bounded below the cell priority is in $(.3,.4)$ and these witnesses precede it, and at least $b/3$ column choices are still available. For the last condition one can use just concentration of the number of other cells of that column seen, with at most three additional cells forced earlier. Averaging and summing, the divergence of $\xi$ from $\mathcal U$ is at least $c(\log n)\mathbb E_\xi L_{\rm bad}-O(n^{.9})$, giving <a href="#tra:asymmetric:eq7" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:asymmetric:eq7">[tra:asymmetric:eq7]</a>, for example by taking $\xi$ the exponential tilt. Hence for our possibly nonuniform column laws, by Hölder (with exponent $c\log n$ on $\exp L_{\rm bad}$, and using density at most $D_L$ of the product law), $$\log\mathbb E\exp L_{\rm bad}
                         \le O(n^{.9}) + \frac{\log D_L}{c\log n}.
                       \label{tra:asymmetric:eq8}$$

The short-cycle estimate controls the column geometry. We next condition on that geometry and expose the row permutations; the restriction to edges belonging to neither a parallel pair nor a four-cycle makes the blocking rows distinct.

Fix columns and upper bound the conditional probability $p$ of distinct pairs, assuming it is positive. The conditional law of row assignments **given** distinct pairs has divergence $-\log p$ from the product of the original row laws. Reveal rows in a random order, again using independent uniform priorities. At row $i$, a conditional divergence term is at least minus log of the original row-law mass of candidates fitting with previously revealed rows (no reused pairs), since the conditional law is supported on such candidates.

To bound these masses, fix any full realization from the law given distinct pairs. In row $i$ let $g_i$ be the number of cells whose column-array edge is not bad. For each such cell $ij$ where a candidate for the row changes the $h$-label, the new pair (new $h$, $l_{ij}$) occurs in the full realization and must occur on some other row (as $l_{ij}$ doesn’t repeat within row $i$). Moreover all the blocking rows identified this way for the candidate are distinct: otherwise two such $l$ values connect row $i$ and another row by a 4-cycle. If $v_i$ is the priority of $i$, put $$x=\min\{-\log(1-v_i), .25\log a\}.$$ Thus for a given candidate matching the realized row permutation at $M$ cells (total matches), the probability over remaining priorities of fitting is at most $\exp(-x g_i+x M)$, since none of the blocking rows can have come before it. So the expected log of the mass fitting, given the realization and $v_i$, by Jensen is at most $$-x g_i + \log\mathbb E_{\nu_i}\exp(xM)$$ where $\nu_i$ is the original candidate law on row $i$. For uniform permutations the log of the moment $\mathbb E\exp(tM)$, $t\ge 0$, is at most $\exp(t)-1$, by counting subsets of matches. Thus by Hölder using exponent $.5(\log a)/x$ on the moment function for $x>0$, we get $$\log\mathbb E_{\nu_i}\exp(xM)
                      \le \frac{2x}{\log a}(\log D_i + a^{.5}).$$ We integrate these log mass bounds keeping in mind $\mathbb E x=1-a^{-1/4}$. They apply uniformly when histories are taken from the full law conditioned on distinct pairs (which can be sampled independently of the priorities). So by the divergence bound for $-\log p$, $$\log p
                 \le -(1-a^{-1/4})(n-L_{\rm bad})
                       +\frac{2}{\log a}\left(\log D_H+b a^{.5}\right)
                 \le -n+ L_{\rm bad} + O(n^{.98})
                                +\frac{C}{\log n}\log D_H.$$ This along with <a href="#tra:asymmetric:eq8" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:asymmetric:eq8">[tra:asymmetric:eq8]</a> proves <a href="#tra:asymmetric:eq6" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:asymmetric:eq6">[tra:asymmetric:eq6]</a>. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-tra-asymmetric-projection-crossing-statement"></a>
<div id="tra:asymmetric:projection-crossing-statement" class="corollary">

<a id="tra:asymmetric:eq9"></a>
**Corollary 41**. *<span id="tra:asymmetric:projection-crossing" label="tra:asymmetric:projection-crossing"></span> We apply the estimate to products of group projections. Use $R$ and $Y$ for the subgroups of $S_n$ permuting within rows and within columns, respectively. For each row of size $a$, let $P_i$ be an orthogonal projection in its group algebra supported just on one irrep $\mu_i$, of rank $r_i>0$ there (so acting on the regular representation, this block action is repeated with multiplicity $d_{\mu_i}$). Put $D_i=d_{\mu_i}r_i$. Likewise take projections for the columns in their group algebras with $D'_j$ defined similarly. Write $P_R,P_Y$ for the two product projections, viewed also in the group algebra of $S_n$. On its regular representation, $$\|P_Y P_R\|_4^4
                  \le \exp(C n^{.98})\,
                         \left(\prod_i D_i \prod_j D'_j\right)^{1+C/\log n}
                        \label{tra:asymmetric:eq9}$$ for an absolute $C$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-tra-asymmetric-projection-crossing-statement"><summary>Proof of stmt-tra-asymmetric-projection-crossing-statement</summary>

*Proof.* <span id="tra:asymmetric:projection-crossing-proof" label="tra:asymmetric:projection-crossing-proof"></span> <span id="tra:asymmetric:projection-crossing-proof-details" label="tra:asymmetric:projection-crossing-proof-details"></span> Apply Lemma <a href="#lem:coefficient-compatibility" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:coefficient-compatibility">14</a> with the line projections as its positive operators. Their regular ranks and squared masses are $D_i=d_{\mu_i}r_i$ and $D'_j$, so the normalized squared coefficient densities have these same caps. At an intermediate cell between row action $r$ and column action $y$, the column of origin is given by $r^{-1}$ and the row of destination by $y$. Thus opposite-order routing is exactly the distinct-pair event in Proposition <a href="#tra:asymmetric:compatibility" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="tra:asymmetric:compatibility">[tra:asymmetric:compatibility]</a>; inversion preserves the coefficient caps. The lemma and <a href="#tra:asymmetric:eq6" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:asymmetric:eq6">[tra:asymmetric:eq6]</a> give $$\|P_YP_R\|_4^4
 \le\frac{n!}{|R||Y|}
       \left(\prod_iD_i\prod_jD'_j\right)
       \exp\left\{-n+Cn^{.98}
          +\frac{C}{\log n}\log\left(\prod_iD_i\prod_jD'_j\right)\right\}.$$ Finally $n!/(|R||Y|)=n!/((a!)^b(b!)^a)\le e^{n+O(\log n)}$, which proves <a href="#tra:asymmetric:eq9" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:asymmetric:eq9">[tra:asymmetric:eq9]</a>. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-42"></a>
#### Spectral integrals with a dimension cutoff

<a id="stmt-tra-asymmetric-trace-statement"></a>
<div id="tra:asymmetric:trace-statement" class="theorem">

<a id="tra:asymmetric:eq10"></a>
**Theorem 42**. *<span id="tra:asymmetric:trace" label="tra:asymmetric:trace"></span> We prove that for each sweep size there is $p_n\ge 4$, all bounded above by an absolute constant, such that $$d_\lambda\,{\rm Tr}|T_n(\lambda)|^{p_n}
                            \ \le\ \exp(n^{.99})
                     \qquad\text{for all }\lambda.
                          \label{tra:asymmetric:eq10}$$ For all sufficiently large $n$, the proof also bounds the complete regular Schatten power by $\exp(n^{.99})$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-tra-asymmetric-trace-statement"><summary>Proof of stmt-tra-asymmetric-trace-statement</summary>

*Proof.* <span id="tra:asymmetric:trace-proof" label="tra:asymmetric:trace-proof"></span> <span id="tra:asymmetric:spectral-integral-recursion" label="tra:asymmetric:spectral-integral-recursion"></span> Let $B\ge 1$ be a fixed constant sufficiently large for <a href="#tra:asymmetric:eq9" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:asymmetric:eq9">[tra:asymmetric:eq9]</a>, so we can use exponent $\Gamma_n=1+B/\log n$ in that bound. We use a sufficiently large absolute cutoff $n_0$, which can be taken above all fixed thresholds as needed in the proof below (in particular the estimates requiring sufficiently large sizes in the induction step will not depend on the base choice of power). Choose $p_{\rm base}\ge \max\{4,p_*\}$, also sufficiently large to make the left side of <a href="#tra:asymmetric:eq10" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:asymmetric:eq10">[tra:asymmetric:eq10]</a> with $p_{\rm base}$ at most 1 for every size up to the cutoff; this is possible by strict contraction on nontrivial sectors. Use $p_{\rm base}$ up to the cutoff. Above, with $a,b$ from the grid estimate, set $$p_n=\left(1+\frac{B+1}{\log n}\right)\max(p_a,p_b).$$ This is bounded absolutely: down any recursion path above the cutoff, the logs of sizes decrease by at least a constant factor (i.e. next at most, say, .95 times the current log), so the sum of their reciprocals there is bounded.

<a id="tra:asymmetric:eq11"></a>
Split the coordinates into the first $\log_2 a$ and the remaining $\log_2 b$, arranging the wires so that $T_n=T_Y T_R$ with $T_R$ a product over rows of copies of $T_a$, and $T_Y$ likewise over columns with $T_b$. Use the ambient regular representation. Put $X=|T_Y|,\ Z=|T_R^*|$. We can drop outer unitary polar factors, and use $$\|T_n\|_{p_n}^{p_n}
                     \le \big\|X^{p_n/4} Z^{p_n/4}\big\|_4^4 .
                           \label{tra:asymmetric:eq11}$$ This is Lemma <a href="#lem:positive-power-comparison" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:positive-power-comparison">9</a> with $P=p_n$ and $q=4$.

<a id="tra:asymmetric:eq12"></a>
The positive powers on the right factor as corresponding products commuting within the line subgroups (row factors amongst themselves, and likewise columns), since the operations factor in the respective subgroup algebras and lift to the ambient group algebra. Write $p=p_n$.
