On a line of size $m$ ($a$ or $b$), according to orientation, use the spectral projections within irrep $\mu$ of that group’s $|T_m|$ or $|T_m^*|$; write $E_{\mu,t}$ for the projection for singular values at least $t>0$ (zero on other irreps), of rank $r_\mu(t)$ on the irrep. The line power for <a href="#tra:asymmetric:eq11" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:asymmetric:eq11">[tra:asymmetric:eq11]</a> is $$\sum_\mu \int_0^1 \frac{p}{4}\,t^{p/4-1} E_{\mu,t}\,dt$$ lifted as an element of the corresponding group algebra. Expand in all lines and use the triangle inequality and <a href="#tra:asymmetric:eq9" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:asymmetric:eq9">[tra:asymmetric:eq9]</a> on the right of <a href="#tra:asymmetric:eq11" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:asymmetric:eq11">[tra:asymmetric:eq11]</a>. This gives $$\|T_n\|_{p}^{p}
   \le \exp(C n^{.98})
        \prod_{\text{lines}}
        \left(\sum_\mu \int_0^1
             \frac{p}{4}\,t^{p/4-1}
             \big(d_\mu r_\mu(t)\big)^{\Gamma_n/4}\,dt\right)^4 .
                  \label{tra:asymmetric:eq12}$$

The spectral support cutoff supplies a negative power of a large child dimension. This compensates for the number of local partition types: a slight surplus in the parent exponent becomes a dimension saving because the integral ends before $t=1$. We show that each integral in <a href="#tra:asymmetric:eq12" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:asymmetric:eq12">[tra:asymmetric:eq12]</a> is $O(\log n)$. Write $W=d_\mu {\rm Tr}|T_m(\mu)|^{p_m}$. Then $$d_\mu r_\mu(t)\le W t^{-p_m},\qquad
         r_\mu(t)=0\ \text{ if }\ t>(W/d_\mu)^{1/p_m}.$$ If $W\le1$ then simply integrating with the first bound gives at most $p/(p-\Gamma_n p_m)=O(\log n)$. This applies for sizes up to the cutoff, and also in larger sizes for the trivial irrep, for the cases from <a href="#tra:asymmetric:eq1" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:asymmetric:eq1">[tra:asymmetric:eq1]</a>, and for the sectors killed by the pair layer. For the remaining cases, we can use $W\le H=\exp(m^{.99})$ inductively and have $\log d_\mu\ge m^{.995}$ by <a href="#tra:asymmetric:eq5" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:asymmetric:eq5">[tra:asymmetric:eq5]</a>. Using the support bound as well gives at most $$\frac{p}{p-\Gamma_n p_m}
                   H^{\Gamma_n/4} (H/d_\mu)^{(p/p_m-\Gamma_n)/4}.$$ Since $p/p_m-\Gamma_n\ge 1/\log n$, this is $O(\log n)$ as claimed (for $m$ above the cutoff), using $m^{.995}\gg m^{.99}\log n$ for large sizes here, as $\log n=O(\log m)$.

The count of partitions of $m$ is at most $\exp(O(\sqrt m\log(m+1)))$, for example by describing rows and columns out from the diagonal. Therefore <a href="#tra:asymmetric:eq12" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:asymmetric:eq12">[tra:asymmetric:eq12]</a> with $b$ lines of size $a$ and $a$ lines of size $b$ yields $$\|T_n\|_p^p\le \exp(n^{.99}),$$ since $b\sqrt{a}=O(n^{.95})$, $a\sqrt{b}=O(n^{.55})$. All the estimates needed here for sufficiently large $n$ have constants independent of $p_{\rm base}$, so a fixed cutoff as specified suffices. We have bounded the regular-representation sum, proving in particular <a href="#tra:asymmetric:eq10" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:asymmetric:eq10">[tra:asymmetric:eq10]</a> and closing the induction. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-tra-asymmetric-mixing"></a>
<div id="tra:asymmetric:mixing" class="corollary">

**Corollary 43** (Vanishing regular remainder). *Let $p^*=\sup_n p_n<\infty$ be the bound obtained above and let $\Pi$ be uniform averaging. For every integer $j\ge2p^*$, $\|T_n^j-\Pi\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2\longrightarrow0$ as $n\to\infty$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-tra-asymmetric-mixing"><summary>Proof of stmt-tra-asymmetric-mixing</summary>

*Proof.* <span id="tra:asymmetric:mixing-proof" label="tra:asymmetric:mixing-proof"></span> <span id="tra:asymmetric:fourier-completion" label="tra:asymmetric:fourier-completion"></span> Finally take a constant integer number of sweeps $j$ at least twice the upper bound on the $p_n$’s. For nontrivial sectors with $1\le k\le n^{.995}$, <a href="#tra:asymmetric:eq1" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:asymmetric:eq1">[tra:asymmetric:eq1]</a> shows for large sizes $$d_\lambda \| T_n(\lambda)^j \|_2^2
                   \le d_\lambda^2 \| T_n(\lambda)\|_{\rm op}^{2j}
                   \le d_\lambda^2 (n^{-10k}/d_\lambda)^4$$ where the first norm after the dimension factor is Hilbert-Schmidt. This is negligible even summed (there are at most $2^k$ partitions for a given $k$). For remaining sectors not already killed we similarly have by <a href="#tra:asymmetric:eq10" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:asymmetric:eq10">[tra:asymmetric:eq10]</a> $$d_\lambda \| T_n(\lambda)^j\|_2^2
                  \le d_\lambda^2 (\exp(n^{.99})/d_\lambda)^4$$ which by <a href="#tra:asymmetric:eq5" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:asymmetric:eq5">[tra:asymmetric:eq5]</a> is again negligible summed over partitions. Thus the squared Hilbert-Schmidt norm in the regular representation of $T_n^j$ minus uniform averaging tends to zero. The identification with the squared $L^2$ distance of the permutation density is the one in Proposition <a href="#e:nonnormal-moment-conversion" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="e:nonnormal-moment-conversion">16</a>. All powers above are controlled by operator submultiplicativity; no normality of $T_n$ is required. ◻

</details>

<a id="tra:projection-deletion"></a>
### Representation level under coordinate deletion

We turn from the choice of entropy law to the sparse representation input. The first question is how much diagram level can disappear when a coordinate is deleted.

A split into two coordinate halves changes the representation in which a vector is decomposed. The useful quantity here is how much of its original level disappears in that decomposition. For a partition $\lambda\vdash m$, its level is $m-\lambda_1$. We control the loss of level by averaging tuple coordinates while retaining their side assignments. A content formula gives a lower bound for the resulting projection norms; random orientations of the matching pairs give an upper bound. Comparing them supplies a tail estimate for the lost level.

The dense part retains different information: an entropy inequality valid for every joint law supported on compatible row and column moves. Correlations within the column family remain in the entropy budget until the final step. These two estimates give a complete moment recursion below.

Throughout this section $n=2^d$, $d\ge1$, $G_n=S_n$, and $T_n$ is the sweep from Section <a href="#sec:prelim" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:prelim">2</a>. Its regular trace is unnormalized, and one sweep corresponds to $d$ physical shuffles.

<a id="tra:projection-deletion:content-and-injection-preliminaries"></a>
#### The content formula and coordinate deletion

<a id="tra:projection-deletion:eq2"></a>
We use standard facts from complex representation theory of symmetric groups. To specify these: irreducibles are indexed by Young diagrams $\lambda$, have dimension $d_\lambda$ the number of standard tableaux, are self-dual, and each has multiplicity $d_\lambda$ in the regular representation. The level for $G_m$ is $m-\lambda_1$. We will use the Pieri rule (special case of Young diagram induction/restriction, or the Littlewood-Richardson rule): the possible types $\rho$ of $G_l$ paired with the trivial representation of $G_{m-l}$ when restricting a type $\lambda$ to $G_l\times G_{m-l}$ are obtained by removing a horizontal strip of size $m-l$ from $\lambda$, with multiplicity one. We also use the content formula (equivalently the Young–Jucys–Murphy formula) for the sum of transpositions (Vershik and Okounkov 2005, Eq. (2.1), Proposition 5.3, Theorem 5.8) <a id="pm-cite-25"></a>[[VershikOkounkov2005](#ref-VershikOkounkov2005)]. Thus the element $\sum_{1\le h<i\le m}(1-(hi))$ acts on type $\lambda$ by $$D_m(\lambda)=\binom m2-\sum_{(u,v)\in\lambda}(v-u)
\label{tra:projection-deletion:eq2}$$ where $u,v$ are row and column.

The representation on ordered injections (ordered distinct sites) of length $l$ contains only types of level at most $l$; a type of level $l$ does occur, by Pieri taking $\rho=(\lambda_2,\lambda_3,\ldots)$. These statements use the realization as functions of a permutation invariant under the right group on $m-l$ indices, with $G_m$ acting on the left; the right $G_l$ acting on the length-$l$ ordering thus has types given by Pieri in each left isotypic component. In particular, in the realization of level $l$ by functions of $l$ distinct sites, summing out any one of the $l$ sites (others fixed) gives zero since that projection is equivariant with image in functions of $l-1$ sites.

<a id="stmt-tra-projection-deletion-level-statement"></a>
<div id="tra:projection-deletion:level-statement" class="proposition">

<a id="tra:projection-deletion:eq3"></a>
**Proposition 44**. *<span id="tra:projection-deletion:level" label="tra:projection-deletion:level"></span> There are absolute $\alpha>0$, $M_0<\infty$, and $0<h<1$, with $$\|T_n\|_\lambda^2\ \le\ h\left(\frac{M_0 k}{n}\right)^{\alpha k}, \qquad k=n-\lambda_1\ge 1,
\label{tra:projection-deletion:eq3}$$ where the norm is operator norm on the indicated representation.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-tra-projection-deletion-level-statement"><summary>Proof of stmt-tra-projection-deletion-level-statement</summary>

*Proof.* <span id="tra:projection-deletion:level-proof" label="tra:projection-deletion:level-proof"></span> <span id="tra:projection-deletion:random-split-deletion-proof" label="tra:projection-deletion:random-split-deletion-proof"></span> It suffices to obtain a nontrivial estimate when $k/n$ is sufficiently small; outside that range, choosing $M_0$ large will make the right side at least one. For $k=1$ the norm is zero: on single-site functions the switches average each bit, giving global averaging as the product.

We induct on the number of coordinates. The main step is a tail bound for the level lost after the first matching projection. Once this bound is established, we will check the constants in the norm recursion.

For induction, write $n=2m$, use the pairs of a dimension for the rightmost projection in $T_n$, and call their flip subgroup $K$, with projection $P_K$. There are two sides of size $m$, with the sites of each pair in opposite sides. The other factors act separately in these two sides, so that $$T_n=(T_m\otimes T_m)P_K,$$ with the tensor product here in the subgroup algebra of $G_m\times G_m$. We use level $k$ realized on the injection tuples $x=(x_1,\ldots,x_k)$. It suffices to bound the squared norm after the two side operators starting with a $K$-invariant unit vector $f$ of our type there. Norms of tuple functions can use uniform counting probability. Such $f$ has zero sum in each of its coordinates as explained above.

Restrict $f$ to the different assignments of the $k$ indices to sides, with $j$ indices in the first side for a given assignment. Decompose in types within the two sides, of levels $s_1,s_2$, where $s_1\le j$, $s_2\le k-j$. We get a probability law on these data by squared norms of the orthogonal parts. Under it put $R=k-s_1-s_2$. We give two controls on this law:

- $j$ has subgaussian tails around $k/2$, in particular $\Pr(|j-k/2|\ge t)\le 2\exp(-2t^2/k)$, and $\Pr(j=0\ \text{or}\ k)\le 2^{1-k}$.

- For $k/n$ sufficiently small, there is an absolute $C_0$ such that

<a id="tra:projection-deletion:eq4"></a>
$$\Pr(R\ge r)\ \le\ (C_0 k/n)^{r/2},\qquad 1\le r\le k .
\label{tra:projection-deletion:eq4}$$

The first property follows from $K$-invariance and averaging by randomizing the pair orientations for the side assignment. Each tuple then uses some double-occupied pairs contributing one index each in the first side, and singles with independent fair side assignment.

To prove <a href="#tra:projection-deletion:eq4" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:projection-deletion:eq4">[tra:projection-deletion:eq4]</a>, consider projections indexed by sets $I$ of $r$ indices to be ignored, that is, average the positions of those indices knowing the positions of the other indices and **the sides of all indices**. Write these as $L_I$. All these averages use the uniform injection law conditioned on the complete side-assignment vector. When an index is deleted, its side remains part of the conditioning and only its position is integrated out. Successive deletions are therefore conditional expectations onto nested sigma-algebras: their composition is the single average over the deleted set. We apply the one-slot bound on each resulting shorter tuple space, retaining the same two left representation types.

<a id="tra:projection-deletion:eq5"></a>
We first record why $$\sum_{|I|=r}\|L_I f\|^2\ \ge\ 2^{-r}\Pr(R\ge r)
\label{tra:projection-deletion:eq5}$$ when $k/n$ is sufficiently small. Work conditionally on assigned sides. Within one side with a tuple of $l\le k$ positions and left type $\mu$ of level $s$, the sum of the projections which average out one coordinate has eigenvalues $$l-\frac{D_m(\mu)-D_l(\rho)}{m-l+1}$$ on the corresponding right types $\rho$ described by Pieri. Indeed the single-coordinate average for coordinate $i$, on functions of a permutation, acts on the right by $(1+\sum_{l<q\le m}(iq))/(m-l+1)$. Sum over $i\le l$, and use <a href="#tra:projection-deletion:eq2" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:projection-deletion:eq2">[tra:projection-deletion:eq2]</a> and invariance on the right under $G_{m-l}$. Now $\rho$ contains the diagram $\bar\mu=(\mu_2,\mu_3,\ldots)$ since $\mu/\rho$ is a horizontal strip. Thus $D_l(\rho)\ge D_s(\bar\mu)$ by adding boxes (each addition to size $v$ to go to size $v+1$ has content at most $v$). Also $D_m(\mu)-D_s(\bar\mu)=(m-s+1)s$. This gives the projection sum lower bound $$(l-s)\left(1-\frac{s}{m-l+1}\right)\ \ge\ (l-s)/2.$$ It holds also with zero indices and the trivial type. For both sides together, summing over the coordinate to remove thus gives squared norms summing to at least half the excess of current tuple length over total level, times the squared norm before removal. After an averaging we can work on the shorter tuples with their marginal law; the averaging preserves the left types when nonzero. On a component of total level $k-R$, iterating this bound through $r$ successive deletions gives $2^{-r}(R)_r$ times the original squared norm, where $(R)_r=R(R-1)\cdots(R-r+1)$. At each stage the conditional expectation acts on the shorter tuple space, with all side assignments retained. The tower property identifies the result with averaging all removed coordinates, and each set $I$ is counted $r!$ times through its possible deletion orders. After division by $r!$, the lower bound is $2^{-r}\binom Rr$, which is at least $2^{-r}$ for $R\ge r$. Summing the components proves <a href="#tra:projection-deletion:eq5" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:projection-deletion:eq5">[tra:projection-deletion:eq5]</a>. All projections in <a href="#tra:projection-deletion:eq5" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:projection-deletion:eq5">[tra:projection-deletion:eq5]</a> respect assignments and the left types of the side groups.

We have expressed a large loss of level as a large sum of coordinate-projection norms. We now bound the same sum from above using the matching-pair symmetries of $f$.

<a id="tra:projection-deletion:eq6"></a>
For the upper bound on the left hand side of <a href="#tra:projection-deletion:eq5" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:projection-deletion:eq5">[tra:projection-deletion:eq5]</a>, we can average it with the side partition randomized by $K$, because $f$ is invariant under $K$. Write $\epsilon(x_i)$ for the side sign of the position $x_i$ under the random orientations. Given the retained positions $z$, the numerator sum in an average over the other positions constrained by a specified vector of side signs $(\eta_i)_{i\in I}$ equals $$\sum_{x|z} f(x)\prod_{i\in I}\frac{1+\eta_i\epsilon(x_i)}{2}
=2^{-r}\left(\prod_{i\in I}\eta_i\right)\sum_{x|z} f(x)\prod_{i\in I}\epsilon(x_i),
\label{tra:projection-deletion:eq6}$$ where $x|z$ indicates all distinct-site extensions. The equality uses the zero sums. In computing the squared norm, we sum squared absolute numerator sums divided by the number of extensions with the given side constraints, over $z$ and $(\eta_i)$, with the overall tuple space normalization. These denominators are at least $(m-k)^r$. Thus we can use this lower bound before expanding the averaged squares on the right in <a href="#tra:projection-deletion:eq6" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:projection-deletion:eq6">[tra:projection-deletion:eq6]</a>.

Two tuples in that expansion, $x,y$ agreeing off $I$, must among their $I$-entries together hit each pair an even number of times for the sign expectation not to vanish. We bound the resulting nonnegative majorant on absolute values of $f$ by a row sum (the matrix is symmetric). For fixed $x$, classify $I$ as using $u$ single entries in pairs and $v$ doubles, $u+2v=r$, counting just $x_I$. The number of choices of $I$ with these data is at most $k^{u+v}/(u!\,v!)$: choose $v$ full pairs in $x$, then the other entries. For each, the possibilities for $y_I$ are bounded by $2^u r! n^v/v!$, since they have to use the same $u$ singleton pairs, and $v$ doubles. The sum over sign specifications costs $2^r$, with a factor $2^{-2r}$ in the square in <a href="#tra:projection-deletion:eq6" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:projection-deletion:eq6">[tra:projection-deletion:eq6]</a>. It follows, using $r!/(u!v!v!)\le 3^r$, that the left hand side of <a href="#tra:projection-deletion:eq5" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:projection-deletion:eq5">[tra:projection-deletion:eq5]</a> is at most $$\frac{2^{-r}}{(m-k)^r}
\sum_{u+2v=r}\frac{k^{u+v}}{u!\,v!}\cdot\frac{2^u r! n^v}{v!}\ \le\ C_1^r(k/n)^{r/2}$$ for an absolute $C_1$ and $k/n$ sufficiently small. This proves <a href="#tra:projection-deletion:eq4" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:projection-deletion:eq4">[tra:projection-deletion:eq4]</a>.

The lost-level tail <a href="#tra:projection-deletion:eq4" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:projection-deletion:eq4">[tra:projection-deletion:eq4]</a> is now proved. It remains to show that its cost is smaller than the contraction supplied by the two child sweeps.

<a id="tra:projection-deletion:eq7"></a>
<a id="tra:projection-deletion:eq8"></a>
To finish the induction for <a href="#tra:projection-deletion:eq3" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:projection-deletion:eq3">[tra:projection-deletion:eq3]</a>, use the inductive bound in each side (factor 1 for level 0). For the squared output norm, divided by the desired bound, this gives the upper bound by the expectation of $$h^{\#\{i:s_i>0\}-1}
\left(\frac{n}{M_0 k}\right)^{\alpha R}
\exp\left(\alpha\sum_{i=1}^2 s_i\log(2s_i/k)\right),
\label{tra:projection-deletion:eq7}$$ where zero terms in the sum are set to zero. The sum in this exponent before multiplying by $\alpha$ is bounded above by $$C_2\big((j-k/2)^2/k+R\big)
\label{tra:projection-deletion:eq8}$$ for some absolute $C_2$. For $s_1=j,s_2=k-j$ this follows by the binary entropy formula or Taylor expansion near $k/2$, and boundedness away from the middle. If $j/k$ is in $[1/4,3/4]$ and $R< k/8$, changing to $s_i$ changes the terms by at most $O(R)$; outside these conditions the crude upper bound $O(k)$ suffices.

Here are details that constants can be fixed in the induction. Take $h=1/20$, and $\alpha>0$ sufficiently small, with $\alpha<1/4$. On $R=0$ and $k\ge2$, cases with $j=0$ or $k$ contribute to the expectation at most $2^{1-k}2^{\alpha k}\le 0.6$ by making $\alpha$ small. The other cases with $R=0$ contribute at most $2h$, by <a href="#tra:projection-deletion:eq8" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:projection-deletion:eq8">[tra:projection-deletion:eq8]</a> and the subgaussian estimate, which by taking $\alpha$ small gives $\mathbb E \exp(2\alpha C_2(j-k/2)^2/k)\le 2$. For $R=r\ge1$, Cauchy-Schwarz with <a href="#tra:projection-deletion:eq8" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:projection-deletion:eq8">[tra:projection-deletion:eq8]</a>, the same subgaussian estimate, and <a href="#tra:projection-deletion:eq4" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:projection-deletion:eq4">[tra:projection-deletion:eq4]</a> bound the total contribution summed over $r\ge1$, for $M_0\ge1$, by $$\frac{\sqrt 2}{h}\sum_{r\ge1}
\left(e^{C_2\alpha}(n/k)^\alpha (C_0 k/n)^{1/4}\right)^r.$$ Choose $M_0$ so large that whenever $h(M_0 k/n)^{\alpha k}<1$, $k/n$ is small enough to apply all the estimates and make this last contribution at most $1/5$. Thus <a href="#tra:projection-deletion:eq7" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:projection-deletion:eq7">[tra:projection-deletion:eq7]</a> gives the bound required. When $h(M_0 k/n)^{\alpha k}\ge1$ we need no induction by contractivity, and level 1 was settled already. This proves <a href="#tra:projection-deletion:eq3" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:projection-deletion:eq3">[tra:projection-deletion:eq3]</a> (with the recursion starting trivially at a single site). ◻

</details>

<a id="tra:projection-deletion:grid-law-definition"></a>
#### An entropy bound for arbitrary compatible laws

The norm estimate controls low representation levels. For the remaining levels we bound the regular trace using an entropy estimate for an array with $b$ rows and $a$ columns ($ab=n$, $a\le b\le 2a$). We will use it for large $a$. Row switches now mean general row permutations $A=(A_i)_{1\le i\le b}$, each $A_i$ a permutation on $a$; and write $B=(B_c)_{1\le c\le a}$ for column permutations, each on $b$. We compose right-to-left, so $BA$ sends $(i,j)$ to row $B_{A_i(j)}(i)$ and column $A_i(j)$.

Call $(A,B)$ valid if, for each $j$, the values $$B_{A_i(j)}(i),\quad 1\le i\le b$$ are distinct. Consider any probability law $\nu$ supported on valid configurations. Write divergences $D$ with uniform reference as follows:

- $D_{\rm joint}$ for both families together relative to uniform independent permutations,

- $D_{A_i},D_{B_c}$ for individual marginal permutations,

- $D_B$ for the joint marginal on all column permutations relative to their uniform product law.

<a id="stmt-tra-projection-deletion-entropy-statement"></a>
<div id="tra:projection-deletion:entropy-statement" class="proposition">

<a id="tra:projection-deletion:eq9"></a>
**Proposition 45**. *<span id="tra:projection-deletion:entropy" label="tra:projection-deletion:entropy"></span> For every probability law $\nu$ supported on valid configurations, with absolute constants and all sufficiently large $a$, $$D_{\rm joint}
\ \ge\ n-O(n a^{-1/16})
 +\left(1-\frac{C_3}{\log a}\right)\left(\sum_i D_{A_i}+\sum_c D_{B_c}\right).
\label{tra:projection-deletion:eq9}$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-tra-projection-deletion-entropy-statement"><summary>Proof of stmt-tra-projection-deletion-entropy-statement</summary>

<a id="tra:projection-deletion:eq10"></a>
*Proof.* <span id="tra:projection-deletion:entropy-proof" label="tra:projection-deletion:entropy-proof"></span> <span id="tra:projection-deletion:light-atoms-and-exceptional-counts" label="tra:projection-deletion:light-atoms-and-exceptional-counts"></span> For clarity, by entropy chain rules, $$D_{\rm joint}=D_B+\sum_i D_{A_i}+I,\qquad
I=\sum_i H(A_i)-H(A\mid B)
\label{tra:projection-deletion:eq10}$$ with $H$ Shannon entropy. We expose all $B_c$, then the rows $A_i$ in random order given by increasing independent uniform priorities $t_i\in[0,1]$ independent of the configuration. Within each row expose the entries in column index order $j=1,\ldots,a$. The contribution for a cell to $I$ is the expected relative entropy of its full conditional law given the information available before exposure (including the order), relative to $p$, its marginal conditional law based on just the history in the same row. Here both laws are for $A_i(j)$, using $\nu$ to form the laws. These expected contributions sum to $I$.

<a id="tra:projection-deletion:eq11"></a>
For this cell let the light set consist of $c$ with $p(c)\le a^{-1/2}$; denote it by $L$, and use $p_L$ for the conditional probability on $L$ when it has mass. An allowed set is given by the candidates $c$ for which $B_c(i)$ does not appear among the previously exposed rows’ outputs $B_{A_{i'}(j)}(i')$ for this column index $j$. The expected relative entropy for the cell is at least $$\mathbb E\left[\mathbf 1_{\{A_i(j)\in L\}}\big(-\log p_L(\text{allowed set})\big)\right].
\label{tra:projection-deletion:eq11}$$ Indeed one decomposes relative entropy according to whether the entry is light, then keeps only the divergence (weighted by conditional probability) when light, whose support condition gives the log bound. The log expression for the weight only needs to be evaluated when the entry is light and is then finite almost surely.

<a id="tra:projection-deletion:eq12"></a>
<a id="tra:projection-deletion:eq13"></a>
Say a realized cell is good if $A_i(j)\in L$, $p(L)\ge a^{-1/8}$, and $$\#\{c:B_c(i)=B_{A_i(j)}(i)\}\le a^{1/4}.
\label{tra:projection-deletion:eq12}$$ Condition on the realized configuration for a good cell and on $t_i$, but not on the priorities of other rows. Each candidate $c$ giving an output distinct from the actual output is forbidden with probability $t_i$, since precisely one other row gives that candidate output value in column index $j$. The mass under $p_L$ of candidates giving the actual output is at most $a^{-1/8}$, by <a href="#tra:projection-deletion:eq12" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:projection-deletion:eq12">[tra:projection-deletion:eq12]</a> and the bounds defining light and good. Consequently the expected allowed mass is at most $1-t_i+t_i a^{-1/8}$. Notice that goodness and $p_L$ depend on data of the configuration but not on the priorities. By nonnegativity in <a href="#tra:projection-deletion:eq11" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:projection-deletion:eq11">[tra:projection-deletion:eq11]</a> we can restrict there to good cells, and Jensen’s inequality and integration in $t_i$ now yield the lower bound $$\Pr(\text{cell good})\left(1-O(a^{-1/16})\right)
\label{tra:projection-deletion:eq13}$$ for <a href="#tra:projection-deletion:eq11" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:projection-deletion:eq11">[tra:projection-deletion:eq11]</a>. This uses $\int_0^1 -\log(1-t+t a^{-1/8})\,dt \ge 1-O(a^{-1/16})$.

Each good cell has supplied almost one nat of entropy. To obtain a total saving of almost $n$, we must pay for the cells excluded by the three goodness conditions.

<a id="tra:projection-deletion:eq14"></a>
<a id="tra:projection-deletion:eq15"></a>
We detail how the expected number of bad cells is bounded by $$O(n a^{-1/16})+\frac{C_4}{\log a}\left(\sum_i D_{A_i}+D_B\right).
\label{tra:projection-deletion:eq14}$$ For heavy actual entries, consider in each row the exposure under its marginal law, relative to drawing a uniform permutation sequentially. Ignore its last at most $O(a^{3/4})$ cells so that all considered draws have at least $a^{3/4}$ positions left. Under the conditional uniform reference, the set $\{c:p(c)>a^{-1/2}\}$ has probability at most $a^{-1/4}$. For any laws $q,q_0$ the variational inequality for divergence gives, for an event $E$ and $v\ge0$, $$D(q\|q_0)\ge v q(E)-\log(1+q_0(E)(e^v-1)).
\label{tra:projection-deletion:eq15}$$ Applying this conditionally with $v=(\log a)/8$ and summing by the chain rule gives the desired heavy-entry part of <a href="#tra:projection-deletion:eq14" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:projection-deletion:eq14">[tra:projection-deletion:eq14]</a>. Cases with $p(L)<a^{-1/8}$ and a light actual entry have expectation count at most $n a^{-1/8}$ without any entropy cost.

It remains to address <a href="#tra:projection-deletion:eq12" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:projection-deletion:eq12">[tra:projection-deletion:eq12]</a>. Its exceptional count is the same computed over $i,c$ instead of $i,j$, looking at the multiplicity of the value $B_c(i)$ in row $i$ of the column-permutation data. For groups of cells with equal such value and multiplicity $>a^{1/4}$, a constant fraction of each group have already had that value appear at least $a^{1/4}/2$ times in earlier columns (up to harmless rounding, or use threshold $a^{1/4}/3$). Reveal the data of $B$ row by row in deterministic order, with columns in order within each. Ignore rows near the end with fewer than $b a^{-1/8}$ entries remaining available in a uniform column permutation. The conditional uniform reference probability that the revealed value has already appeared at least $a^{1/4}/3$ times within the row is at most $3a^{3/4}/(b a^{-1/8})\le 3a^{-1/8}$. Apply <a href="#tra:projection-deletion:eq15" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:projection-deletion:eq15">[tra:projection-deletion:eq15]</a> with $v=(\log a)/16$ and the chain rule for $D_B$. This proves the remaining exceptional count bound, hence <a href="#tra:projection-deletion:eq14" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:projection-deletion:eq14">[tra:projection-deletion:eq14]</a>.

Summing <a href="#tra:projection-deletion:eq13" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:projection-deletion:eq13">[tra:projection-deletion:eq13]</a> and using <a href="#tra:projection-deletion:eq10" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:projection-deletion:eq10">[tra:projection-deletion:eq10]</a>, <a href="#tra:projection-deletion:eq14" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:projection-deletion:eq14">[tra:projection-deletion:eq14]</a> proves <a href="#tra:projection-deletion:eq9" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:projection-deletion:eq9">[tra:projection-deletion:eq9]</a>, using $D_B\ge\sum_c D_{B_c}$ once the coefficient on $D_B$ is positive. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-tra-projection-deletion-weighted-statement"></a>
<div id="tra:projection-deletion:weighted-statement" class="corollary">

<a id="tra:projection-deletion:eq16"></a>
**Corollary 46**. *<span id="tra:projection-deletion:weighted" label="tra:projection-deletion:weighted"></span> Here is a useful weighted form. Put $\theta=C_3/\log a$ (increasing the absolute constant if needed), so $0<\theta<1$ for sufficiently large $a$. Under uniform independent permutations, for nonnegative functions $z_i$ of a row permutation and $w_c$ of a column permutation, $$\begin{split}
\log\mathbb E_{\rm unif}\left[\mathbf 1_{\rm valid}
       \prod_i z_i(A_i)^2\prod_c w_c(B_c)^2\right]
\ \le\ &-n+O(n a^{-1/16})\\
 &+2\sum_i\log\|z_i\|_{2/(1-\theta)}
    +2\sum_c\log\|w_c\|_{2/(1-\theta)}
\end{split}
\label{tra:projection-deletion:eq16}$$ where the norms are under the marginal uniform probabilities.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-tra-projection-deletion-weighted-statement"><summary>Proof of stmt-tra-projection-deletion-weighted-statement</summary>

*Proof.* <span id="tra:projection-deletion:weighted-proof" label="tra:projection-deletion:weighted-proof"></span> <span id="tra:projection-deletion:weighted-variational-proof" label="tra:projection-deletion:weighted-variational-proof"></span> This is the finite-space entropy–Brascamp–Lieb duality of Carlen and Cordero-Erausquin (Carlen and Cordero-Erausquin 2009, Theorem 2.1) <a id="pm-cite-26"></a>[[CarlenCorderoErausquin2009](#ref-CarlenCorderoErausquin2009)], applied to the compatibility event. We give the specialization to fix the coefficient of every marginal deficit.

The log integral on the left is given by the entropy variational formula, maximizing the expected log product minus $D_{\rm joint}$ over allowed laws supported on valid pairs. After <a href="#tra:projection-deletion:eq9" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:projection-deletion:eq9">[tra:projection-deletion:eq9]</a> the remaining marginal terms are each bounded by the separate variational formulas with coefficient $1-\theta$. Zero weights can also be treated by a limit. ◻

</details>

<a id="tra:projection-deletion:operator-split"></a>
#### The dense trace recursion

We now apply the weighted entropy estimate to coefficient densities of positive powers of the two smaller sweeps. The fourth trace turns their product into the validity constraint just analyzed. Split $d$ into parts as equally as possible for $n=2^d$, thus taking $a=2^{\lfloor d/2\rfloor}$, $b=2^{\lceil d/2\rceil}$. Make the array of cube positions accordingly. In group algebra, $T_n=T^{\rm row}T^{\rm col}$ where the row factor consists of independent runs with operator $T_a$ in every row, and the column factor similarly uses $T_b$. Indeed we just divide the dimensions into two consecutive groups; the grouping and naming is in product-of-operators order here. Put $$X=(T^{\rm row})^*T^{\rm row},\qquad Y=T^{\rm col}(T^{\rm col})^*$$ positive operators. Within the subgroup algebras these are products on separate permutations, with individual operators $X_i$ and $Y_c$ of the forms $T_a^*T_a$ and $T_b T_b^*$, respectively. For traces or norms on subgroup factors we can use their own regular representations. Positive powers stay in the algebra and are likewise products there.

<a id="stmt-tra-projection-deletion-trace-recursion-statement"></a>
<div id="tra:projection-deletion:trace-recursion-statement" class="proposition">

<a id="tra:projection-deletion:eq17"></a>
<a id="tra:projection-deletion:eq18"></a>
**Proposition 47**. *<span id="tra:projection-deletion:recursion" label="tra:projection-deletion:recursion"></span> Suppose for some $p\ge2$ we have $$\operatorname{Tr}_{G_a}|T_a|^{2p}\le 2,\qquad
\operatorname{Tr}_{G_b}|T_b|^{2p}\le 2.
\label{tra:projection-deletion:eq17}$$ Let $p'=p(1+\theta)$ with $\theta$ as in <a href="#tra:projection-deletion:eq16" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:projection-deletion:eq16">[tra:projection-deletion:eq16]</a>. We claim $$\log\operatorname{Tr}_{G_n}|T_n|^{2p'}\ \le\ O(n a^{-1/16}+\sqrt n\log n).
\label{tra:projection-deletion:eq18}$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-tra-projection-deletion-trace-recursion-statement"><summary>Proof of stmt-tra-projection-deletion-trace-recursion-statement</summary>

<a id="tra:projection-deletion:eq19"></a>
*Proof.* <span id="tra:projection-deletion:recursion-proof" label="tra:projection-deletion:recursion-proof"></span> <span id="tra:projection-deletion:interpolation-and-fourth-trace" label="tra:projection-deletion:interpolation-and-fourth-trace"></span> First, a positive-matrix trace comparison gives $$\operatorname{Tr}|T_n|^{2p'}\ \le\ 
\operatorname{Tr}\left(X^{p'/2}Y^{p'/2}X^{p'/2}Y^{p'/2}\right).
\label{tra:projection-deletion:eq19}$$ Apply Lemma <a href="#lem:positive-power-comparison" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:positive-power-comparison">9</a> with $A_2=T^{\rm row}$, $A_1=T^{\rm col}$, $P=2p'$ and $q=4$. Then $X=|A_2|^2$, $Y=|A_1^*|^2$, giving exactly <a href="#tra:projection-deletion:eq19" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:projection-deletion:eq19">[tra:projection-deletion:eq19]</a>.

<a id="tra:projection-deletion:eq20"></a>
Write $x(A)=\prod_i x_i(A_i)$ for the coefficients as a density relative to uniform row permutations of $X^{p'/2}$; similarly $y(B)=\prod_c y_c(B_c)$ for $Y^{p'/2}$. The individual positive line operators are $X_i^{p'/2}$ and $Y_c^{p'/2}$. Applying Lemma <a href="#lem:coefficient-compatibility" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:coefficient-compatibility">14</a> to these operators, before normalizing their squared coefficient masses, gives $$\operatorname{Tr}|T_n|^{2p'}\ \le\
\frac{n!}{(a!)^b (b!)^a}
  \ \mathbb E_{\rm unif}\left[\mathbf 1_{\rm valid}|x(A)|^2 |y(B)|^2\right].
\label{tra:projection-deletion:eq20}$$

For the line norms we use Lemma <a href="#lem:inverse-fourier-bound" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:inverse-fourier-bound">10</a> in each subgroup’s own regular representation. With $q=2/(1+\theta)$, the Schatten $q$ norm of $X_i^{p'/2}$ in its own regular representation is at most $2^{1/q}$ by <a href="#tra:projection-deletion:eq17" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:projection-deletion:eq17">[tra:projection-deletion:eq17]</a>, and similarly for $Y_c^{p'/2}$. Consequently the individual densities in <a href="#tra:projection-deletion:eq20" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:projection-deletion:eq20">[tra:projection-deletion:eq20]</a> have the needed $2/(1-\theta)$-norms bounded by 2. Apply <a href="#tra:projection-deletion:eq16" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:projection-deletion:eq16">[tra:projection-deletion:eq16]</a> to their absolute values. Since by Stirling’s estimate $$\log\left(\frac{n!}{(a!)^b(b!)^a}\right)=n+O(\sqrt n\log n),$$ <a href="#tra:projection-deletion:eq20" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:projection-deletion:eq20">[tra:projection-deletion:eq20]</a> proves <a href="#tra:projection-deletion:eq18" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:projection-deletion:eq18">[tra:projection-deletion:eq18]</a>. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-tra-projection-deletion-main-statement"></a>
<div id="tra:projection-deletion:main-statement" class="theorem">

<a id="tra:projection-deletion:eq1"></a>
**Theorem 48**. *<span id="tra:projection-deletion:moment" label="tra:projection-deletion:moment"></span> There are real numbers $p_n\ge2$, indexed by dyadic $n\ge2$, with $\sup_n p_n<\infty$ such that $$\operatorname{Tr}_{G_n}|T_n|^{2p_n}\ \le\ 1+\tfrac{1}{8}.
\label{tra:projection-deletion:eq1}$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-tra-projection-deletion-main-statement"><summary>Proof of stmt-tra-projection-deletion-main-statement</summary>

*Proof of Theorem <a href="#tra:projection-deletion:moment" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="tra:projection-deletion:moment">[tra:projection-deletion:moment]</a>.* <span id="tra:projection-deletion:moment-induction-and-completion" label="tra:projection-deletion:moment-induction-and-completion"></span> The rectangle estimate leaves a subexponential regular-trace error. We remove it by separating the low levels, controlled by Proposition <a href="#tra:projection-deletion:level" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="tra:projection-deletion:level">[tra:projection-deletion:level]</a>, from the higher levels, whose regular multiplicities are large. For large $n$, use $n^{0.995}$ as the threshold for level. On all types with $1\le k\le n^{0.995}$, we already have, independently of <a href="#tra:projection-deletion:eq17" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:projection-deletion:eq17">[tra:projection-deletion:eq17]</a>, enough decay for the trace estimate <a href="#tra:projection-deletion:eq1" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:projection-deletion:eq1">[tra:projection-deletion:eq1]</a> at a sufficiently large absolute power $p_{\rm low}$. Indeed each $d_\lambda\le n^k$ by occurrence on injection tuples, and there are at most $2^k$ diagrams at that level. Using <a href="#tra:projection-deletion:eq3" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:projection-deletion:eq3">[tra:projection-deletion:eq3]</a>, for $n$ sufficiently large and any $s\ge p_{\rm low}$, the total contribution of these types to $\operatorname{Tr}|T_n|^{2s}$ is $o(1)$; for example $M_0 k/n\le n^{-0.004}$ there, so we can sum the bounds $2^k n^{2k} (n^{-0.004})^{\alpha k p_{\rm low}}$.

<a id="tra:projection-deletion:eq21"></a>
For any type not annihilated by $T_n$, the number of rows of the diagram is at most $n/2$. Indeed it needs invariants for the flip subgroup of one dimension, a product of $n/2$ copies of the two-point symmetric group, so the Pieri rule builds its diagram by adding $n/2$ horizontal strips. For such diagrams with $k> n^{0.995}$ and sufficiently large $n$, we have $$d_\lambda\ \ge\ \exp(c n^{0.995})
\label{tra:projection-deletion:eq21}$$ with absolute $c>0$. One quick count of tableaux is by ordering the boxes according to increasing sum of their two coordinates, with arbitrary order within each antidiagonal. If there are $l$ antidiagonals the factorials of their sizes give a product at least $2^{n-l}$. Here $l=\max_i(i+\lambda_i-1)\le\sqrt n+\max(\lambda_1,n/2)$ since $i\lambda_i\le n$, proving <a href="#tra:projection-deletion:eq21" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:projection-deletion:eq21">[tra:projection-deletion:eq21]</a>.

When <a href="#tra:projection-deletion:eq17" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:projection-deletion:eq17">[tra:projection-deletion:eq17]</a> holds and $n$ is sufficiently large, <a href="#tra:projection-deletion:eq18" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:projection-deletion:eq18">[tra:projection-deletion:eq18]</a> gives $$\operatorname{Tr}|T_n|^{2p'}\le \exp(n^{0.99}).$$ We apply Lemma <a href="#lem:balanced-moment-closure" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:balanced-moment-closure">19</a> with $\nu=2$, $\varepsilon=1/8$ and $P=\max(p_{\rm low},2)$. The low class consists of the first-row levels $1\le k\le n^{0.995}$ together with the annihilated blocks; its contribution is at most $1/16$ above an absolute threshold. The remaining blocks satisfy <a href="#tra:projection-deletion:eq21" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:projection-deletion:eq21">[tra:projection-deletion:eq21]</a>. Thus the parameters in the common lemma are $$E_n=n^{0.99},\qquad H_n=c n^{0.995},\qquad
 \alpha_d=1+C_3/\log a,\qquad \delta_d=1/\log n.$$ The child bound $1+1/8$ implies the bound $2$ required in <a href="#tra:projection-deletion:eq17" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:projection-deletion:eq17">[tra:projection-deletion:eq17]</a>, and all size thresholds are independent of the inherited exponent. Moreover, $$(1+\delta_d)E_n-\delta_dH_n
 =(1+1/\log n)n^{0.99}-c n^{0.995}/\log n\longrightarrow-\infty,$$ while $\alpha_d(1+\delta_d)=1+O(1/d)$. The lemma supplies bounded parameters $p_n$ and proves <a href="#tra:projection-deletion:eq1" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:projection-deletion:eq1">[tra:projection-deletion:eq1]</a>.

Proposition <a href="#e:nonnormal-moment-conversion" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="e:nonnormal-moment-conversion">16</a>, with singular moment exponent $2\sup_n p_n$ and remainder $1/8$, now gives the mixing bound after an absolute number of sweeps. The lower bound in physical shuffle units is Lemma <a href="#lem:support" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:support">[lem:support]</a>. ◻

</details>

<a id="tra:first-interactions"></a>
### First interactions and indexed singular values

Coordinate deletion tracks a representation statistic through a split. The next argument instead stops paths at their first interactions. We combine its sparse norm estimate with a projection overlap bound to retain the singular rank inside each irreducible block.

This method controls every singular index within an irreducible representation. Its sparse argument orders the first interactions of labels and deletes them in reverse order. Its dense argument charges coloring constraints to conditional total correlation. The resulting rank estimate closes under a balanced split of the bit directions.

Write $T_n$ for the sweep operator, $V_\lambda$ for an irreducible representation of $S_n$, and $D_\lambda=\dim V_\lambda$. Each trace is unnormalized. The index in the next theorem belongs to a single irreducible block; its contribution to a regular trace is repeated $D_\lambda$ times. We first control blocks close to the trivial representation directly from their paths. A compatibility estimate then handles the other blocks and permits induction on the bit length.

<a id="stmt-tra-first-interactions-indexed-conclusion"></a>
<div id="tra:first-interactions:indexed-conclusion" class="theorem">

**Theorem 49**. *<span id="tra:first-interactions:singular" label="tra:first-interactions:singular"></span>*

<a id="tra:first-interactions:eq1"></a>
*There is an absolute finite $p_*>0$ such that, for every dyadic $n$, every partition $\lambda\vdash n$, and every $1\le i\le D_\lambda$, $$\label{tra:first-interactions:eq1}
 s_i(T_n(\lambda))\le(D_\lambda i)^{-1/(2p_*)}.$$ The singular values are listed in decreasing order within one copy of $V_\lambda$.*

</div>

<a id="pm-h-48"></a>
#### A sparse estimate by deleting first interactions

A representation whose first row has length $n-k$ first occurs in the action on $k$ ordered distinct cards. On its new part, any term that ignores a card vanishes. This cancellation forces every tracked card to interact with another one. Our immediate task is to show that such complete coverage has small operator norm when $k\le n^{.99}$. The following occupation estimate will control the exceptional starting configurations.

<a id="stmt-grid-occupation"></a>
<div id="grid:occupation" class="lemma">

**Lemma 50** (Occupation bounds for partially coupled paths). *Start a set of $r$ cards at distinct sites of the binary cube and move them by one complete coordinate sweep. Independently, move $s$ further walkers, each by its own fair bit in every coordinate; these walkers may have coincident endpoints. For disjoint sets of sites $A_1,\ldots,A_L$, let $N_i$ count all $r+s$ endpoints in $A_i$, with repetitions counted for the independent walkers. For nonnegative integers $h_i$, $$\mathbb E\prod_i\binom{N_i}{h_i}
 \le\prod_i\frac{((r+s)|A_i|/n)^{h_i}}{h_i!}.$$ In particular the same right side bounds $\Pr\{N_i\ge h_i\text{ for every }i\}$. The assertion also holds with the coordinate order reversed.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-grid-occupation"><summary>Proof of stmt-grid-occupation</summary>

*Proof.* Let $\eta(x)$ be the occupation indicator for the $r$ jointly moved cards, and $p_x=\mathbb E\eta(x)$. At the deterministic initial set, $\mathbb E\prod_{x\in A}\eta(x)\le\prod_{x\in A}p_x$ for every set $A$. A fair switch on $u,v$ preserves this family of inequalities. If $A$ contains neither endpoint there is no change. If it contains one endpoint, averaging the two old inequalities replaces its marginal by $(p_u+p_v)/2$. If it contains both, the occupation product is unchanged and $p_up_v\le((p_u+p_v)/2)^2$. Disjoint switches can be applied successively, proving preservation through the sweep. At its end every $p_x=r/n$, because the endpoint of each individual card is uniform. Summing over distinct tested sites in the disjoint $A_i$ therefore bounds the joint binomial moments for these cards by $\prod_i(r|A_i|/n)^{h_i}/h_i!$.

The independent walkers have multinomial factorial moments bounded by the same expression with $s$ in place of $r$: assign the tested hits to distinct walkers, and use their uniform independent endpoints. Expand each binomial coefficient of the sum of the two counts using Vandermonde’s identity. Independence of the two populations and the binomial theorem replace $r$ and $s$ by $r+s$. This proves the stated bound. No part of this proof depends on which coordinate is updated first. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-tra-first-interactions-sparse-statement"></a>
<div id="tra:first-interactions:sparse-statement" class="lemma">

**Lemma 51**. *<span id="tra:first-interactions:sparse" label="tra:first-interactions:sparse"></span>*

<a id="tra:first-interactions:eq2"></a>
*For some absolute $c_s>0$ and all sufficiently large $n$, if $1\le k=n-\lambda_1\le n^{.99}$, then $$\|T_n(\lambda)\|_{\rm op}\le n^{-c_s k}.\label{tra:first-interactions:eq2}$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-tra-first-interactions-sparse-statement"><summary>Proof of stmt-tra-first-interactions-sparse-statement</summary>

*Proof.* <span id="tra:first-interactions:sparse-proof" label="tra:first-interactions:sparse-proof"></span>

<a id="tra:first-interactions:eq3"></a>
<span id="tra:first-interactions:endpoint-kernel-and-centered-cover" label="tra:first-interactions:endpoint-kernel-and-centered-cover"></span> To see this, take the sweep kernel on $k$-tuples, with row variable $x=(x_1,\ldots,x_k)$ the input tuple and column variable $y$ the output tuple. Actions on tuples, or on functions of them, estimate the same singular values on $\lambda$. For two tuple labels $u,v$, set $$h=h(u,v)=\max\{i:(x_u)_i\ne(x_v)_i\},\qquad
 l=l(u,v)=\min\{i:(y_u)_i\ne(y_v)_i\}$$ for distinct tuple entries as here. Define $$w(h,l)=\begin{cases}1& l<h,\\
                                        2& l=h,\\
                                        0& l>h.
                           \end{cases}$$ Then the tuple kernel is $$n^{-k}\prod_{u<v} w(h(u,v),l(u,v)).\label{tra:first-interactions:eq3}$$ Indeed given endpoints, paths replace one bit after another in $x$ by the corresponding bit of $y$. They must remain nonoverlapping as paths through positions. For a pair, if the output bits below $h$ (indices $<h$) agree, the paths would use the same switch at $h$, where output bits must be opposite. When compatible they use either no common switch or that one, by the bit replacement order. Thus pair conditions suffice, and each shared switch gains a factor 2 compared to probabilities for independent paths.

For $J\subset [k]$, put $$Q_J(x,y)=n^{-k}\prod_{\{u,v\}\subset J} w(h(u,v),l(u,v)).$$ This is the restriction (to our distinct tuples) of the kernel using the joint shuffle only on labels in $J$, and placing the other output labels independently uniformly; likewise its transpose is restricted from using the reverse shuffle jointly only on $J$. In particular each of its row and column sums is at most 1. In bounding the block on $\lambda$ we can replace <a href="#tra:first-interactions:eq3" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:first-interactions:eq3">[tra:first-interactions:eq3]</a> by $$Z=\sum_{J\subset[k]}(-1)^{k-|J|}Q_J .$$ Indeed proper-subset terms can be dropped on compression to the $\lambda$-isotypic space. Their images or the images of their transposes are in subspaces of functions depending only on a shorter tuple, which have no $\lambda$ part.

Make the interaction graph on $[k]$ for $(x,y)$ by using an edge for $u,v$ if $(y_u)_i=(y_v)_i$ for all $i<h(u,v)$; the edge time is $h(u,v)$. The sum for $Z$ vanishes if there is an isolated label, by cancellation. Thus it suffices for norm bounds to use nonnegative kernels $Q_J$, summed but restricted by the coverage condition (all labels have an interaction).

<span id="tra:first-interactions:bad-cell-factorial-moments" label="tra:first-interactions:bad-cell-factorial-moments"></span> Put $\epsilon=.01$, so that $k\le n^{1-\epsilon}$, and take $\alpha=\epsilon/2$. We use the dyadic cells from the input hierarchy: a cell of size $2^h$ specifies the bits of index $>h$. For an input $x$, call a label bad if it is in some such cell of size $t$ where the label count $r$ from $x$ satisfies $$r\ge 2,\qquad r> t n^{-\alpha}.$$ Otherwise call the label good. Split rows into bad rows (at least $k/2$ bad labels) and the other rows (called good rows).

Here are two probability bounds for this split.

<a id="tra:first-interactions:eq4"></a>
- Given $y$, the column sum of $Q_J$ over bad rows is $n^{-\Omega(k)}$, meaning bounded by $n^{-c k}$ for an absolute $c>0$ for all sufficiently large $n$, uniformly. In the transpose experiment the output considered here is $x$. We will use factorial moment bounds on counts in cells. Lemma <a href="#grid:occupation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="grid:occupation">50</a>, with $r=|J|$ and $s=k-|J|$, gives, for disjoint cells of sizes $t_i$ and required counts $r_i$, $$\label{tra:first-interactions:eq4}
   \Pr\{N_i\ge r_i\text{ for all }i\}
   \le\prod_i\frac{(kt_i/n)^{r_i}}{r_i!}.$$ This bound is used before restriction to distinct output tuples; that restriction can only decrease a column sum of the nonnegative kernel.

  A bad row gives a family of disjoint cells (take maximal ones from the bad-label definition), where $$r_i\ge 2,\qquad t_i/r_i\le n^\alpha,\qquad
                             k/2\le R_0=\sum r_i\le k$$ with $r_i$ their counts. We spell out a union bound. For choices of ordered sizes and counts, multiplying <a href="#tra:first-interactions:eq4" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:first-interactions:eq4">[tra:first-interactions:eq4]</a> by $\prod_i n/t_i$ allows the choices of locations. Using $r!\ge(r/e)^r$, the result is at most $$\prod_i \left[e^{r_i}\frac{k}{r_i}
                     \left(\frac{k t_i}{n r_i}\right)^{r_i-1}\right]
                 \le e^k k^L n^{-(\epsilon-\alpha)(R_0-L)}.$$ In summing over ordered lists we divide by $L!$, since we seek unordered families of distinct cells. The factor $k^L/L!$ is at most $e^k$. The remaining number of size and count lists over lengths and totals is bounded by $(C(d+1))^{Ck}$ using compositions, for some absolute $C$. Since $R_0-L\ge R_0/2\ge k/4$, this proves the column bound.

<span id="tra:first-interactions:first-meeting-deletion" label="tra:first-interactions:first-meeting-deletion"></span>

- Given $x$ in a good row, the row sum of $Q_J$ subject to coverage is $n^{-\Omega(k)}$, uniformly. Simulate $Q_J$ before restriction by using independent personal fair bits for each label at each time. Labels outside $J$ just use these bits; labels in $J$ also do, except that when two in $J$ use the same switch we use one of their bits (chosen, say, by label index) and its opposite for the two respective new position bits. This generates the kernel since placements of the $J$ labels need only this joint use of bits, independently at each switch. Only $J$-labels count for this bit-sharing rule.

  We track the first interaction of a label in the interaction graph (now defined by the output bits whether or not all outputs end up distinct). Until its first interaction its output bits come from its own personal bits. Indeed an actual $J$-pair at a switch at time $h$ must have highest differing input bit $h$ and matching lower output bits, as the $J$-positions have stayed distinct.

  If all good labels have interactions, we can select a subset $D$ of them of size at least half the number of good labels, and for each $u\in D$ specify a partner $v(u)$ witnessing its first interaction, so that if the partner also belongs to $D$, its first time is strictly earlier. To justify the selection, look at labels having their first interaction at a given switch, defined by its time $h$, the fixed higher input bits, and the common lower output bits. On either of the two sides of this switch there is at most one label having its first interaction there. Two labels on that same side, arriving with the same lower output bits, would have an interaction at their own highest differing input bit, which would be earlier. Hence at most two have their first interaction there. In case two good labels first interact there, we can omit one to avoid ties; one good label alone with first interaction there needs no omission (partners not required to be selected).

<a id="tra:first-interactions:eq5"></a>
  For fixed specifications with times $h_u=h(u,v(u))$, the probability of these witnesses with the stated first-time property is bounded by $$\prod_{u\in D} 2^{-(h_u-1)}.\label{tra:first-interactions:eq5}$$ To see this without independence assumptions about the partners, take labels in $D$ of largest specified time $h$, and compare with the simulation deleting those labels, using the same personal bits of the rest. On the witness event the rest follow the deletion simulation through time $h-1$, since no deleted label has interacted before then. Earlier witnessing events persist in that simulation. Each deleted label must match its specified partner on the first $h-1$ output bits, and on the event uses personal bits up to then. Its partner belongs to the rest by the selection condition. With the rest’s personal bits given, these necessary matches have probability $2^{-(h-1)}$ per deleted label, independently for the purpose of this bound. This gives <a href="#tra:first-interactions:eq5" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:first-interactions:eq5">[tra:first-interactions:eq5]</a> by successive deletion; equivalently we sum specifications only where within $D$ partners are of strictly earlier specified time.

  For one good label $u$, the sum over possible partners of $2^{-(h(u,v)-1)}$ is at most $2d n^{-\alpha}$. For a contributing level $h$, the cell of size $2^h$ containing $u$ contains a partner and so contains at most $2^h n^{-\alpha}$ labels since $u$ is good. Because in a good row there must be a witness specification with $|D|\ge k/4$ if coverage holds, summing <a href="#tra:first-interactions:eq5" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:first-interactions:eq5">[tra:first-interactions:eq5]</a> over the subsets and partners gives the row bound for large $n$.

For $Z$ we can sum these bounds with a $2^k$ factor. On the good-row portion, one has small row sums in absolute value by the second bound and at most $2^k$ for absolute column sums. On the bad-row portion, the first bound gives small column sums, and row sums in absolute value are at most $2^k$. The row-column sum bound on operator norm now gives $\|Z\|_{\rm op}\le n^{-\Omega(k)}$. This proves <a href="#tra:first-interactions:eq2" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:first-interactions:eq2">[tra:first-interactions:eq2]</a>. ◻

</details>

<a id="tra:first-interactions:balanced-grid-setup"></a>
#### Conditional total correlation in a rectangle

The sparse argument is complete: ignoring any one label kills the new representation level, and the remaining path systems are rare on good rows or on bad columns. We now turn to the large-dimensional blocks. A balanced split reduces them to products of smaller sweep operators. The missing input is a bound on the overlap of their Fourier subspaces, which we obtain by estimating the probability of row–column compatibility. In it we regard positions as an $a\times b$ rectangle, $a b=n$, with $$a,b\in[\sqrt n/\sqrt 2,\sqrt 2\sqrt n].$$ Use subgroups $H,J_0$ of the symmetric group $G$ on the rectangle: $H$ permutes positions separately within each column (so $H=(S_a)^b$ in symmetric group notation), and $J_0$ does so in each row. Below, logs for entropy and estimates are natural. We continue to allow all bound constants to be absolute and to consider sufficiently large sizes.

We will need the following probability estimate.

<a id="stmt-tra-first-interactions-grid-statement"></a>
<div id="tra:first-interactions:grid-statement" class="proposition">

**Proposition 52**. *<span id="tra:first-interactions:grid" label="tra:first-interactions:grid"></span>*

<a id="tra:first-interactions:eq6"></a>
*Draw elements $h\in H$ (column permutations $h_v,\ 1\le v\le b$) and $j\in J_0$ (row permutations $j_r,\ 1\le r\le a$) with all permutations independent, from possibly nonuniform laws. Suppose on each factor the pointwise density versus uniform is bounded, with the product of those upper bounds $e^z$. Then $$\Pr\{ h j\in J_0 H\}
                  \le \exp\{-n+C n^{.98} + C z/\log n\}.\label{tra:first-interactions:eq6}$$ Here $h j$ means apply $j$ and then $h$. The coefficient of $-n$ is essential: the later regular-trace normalization contributes $+n$ to leading order.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-tra-first-interactions-grid-statement"><summary>Proof of stmt-tra-first-interactions-grid-statement</summary>

*Proof.* <span id="tra:first-interactions:grid-proof" label="tra:first-interactions:grid-proof"></span>

<span id="tra:first-interactions:total-correlation-exposure" label="tra:first-interactions:total-correlation-exposure"></span> For given $j$, make a bipartite multigraph between left vertices $u$ and right vertices $v$, both sets indexing columns. Each initial site $(r,u)$ gives an edge, of row $r$, from $u$ to $v=j_r(u)$. Each vertex has degree $a$. Color this edge by $h_v(r)$, a color from $[a]$, so colors are all used once at each right vertex. If $hj\in J_0 H$, every left vertex also sees every color once, since cards of each initial column must go one to each final row. Call this a valid coloring. (This condition also suffices, though necessity is enough.)

Condition the experiment on the event in <a href="#tra:first-interactions:eq6" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:first-interactions:eq6">[tra:first-interactions:eq6]</a>, assuming positive probability. Its log inverse probability is the relative entropy of this new law with respect to the original experiment. Write it as $$L=L_j+L_h+L_{\rm corr},$$ where:

- $L_j$ is the relative entropy paid for the new marginal of $j$;

- $L_h$ is the sum, averaged over this marginal of $j$, of relative entropies paid for the individual column permutation marginals conditional on $j$, versus their original independent laws;

- $L_{\rm corr}$ is the conditional total correlation among the column permutations given $j$, i.e., the relative entropy against the product of their conditional marginals (averaged over $j$).

All are nonnegative. Write $z_j,z_h$ for the parts of $z$ from the row, column factors, respectively. The relative entropy of the new marginal of $j$ versus independent uniform row permutations is at most $L_j+z_j$. The sum of relative entropies of the column permutation marginals given $j$, each versus uniform, is in expectation at most $L_h+z_h$. These comparisons follow from the density upper bounds.

<a id="tra:first-interactions:eq7"></a>
Estimate $L_{\rm corr}$ by exposing right vertices one by one. In this argument we are in the conditioned experiment, in particular the coloring is valid. Fix $j$, and take an order from independent uniform priorities in $[0,1]$ for the right vertices, independent of everything else. By the chain rule, the conditional total correlation is the sum of the mutual informations between each $h_v$ and the preceding $h$-variables (for fixed order, given $j$). Within $h_v$ expose entries in row order $1,\ldots,a$ and use the chain rule again. Consider the entry corresponding to a particular edge, from left vertex $u$ to $v$, and condition also on earlier entries at $v$, but not yet other columns’ information. Denote by $p_c$, $c\in[a]$, the conditional law of this entry. We use mutual information of the color with the preceding vertices, for the conditional law (and average over these conditionings). For a fixed set of preceding vertices, if the color is $c$, none of those vertices can have color $c$ on an edge from $u$. Thus, writing mutual information as the average relative entropy of the preceding vertices’ variables given the color versus their marginal here, a lower bound for this term is $$\sum_c p_c \left(-\log\Pr\{\text{color }c
                           \text{ not used from }u\text{ at preceding vertices}\}\right).\label{tra:first-interactions:eq7}$$ This uses the marginal not given the color inside the $-\log$, with the conditioning on $j$ and earlier entries at $v$ still in force; the bound follows from relative entropy for a law supported on an event.

<a id="tra:first-interactions:eq8"></a>
If $v$’s priority is $t$, average the preceding set over the other priorities. For color $c$, write $$\delta_c=\Pr\{\text{the edge from }u\text{ colored }c\text{ goes to }v\}$$ in the same conditional law not given the entry. Validity implies that the survival probability inside <a href="#tra:first-interactions:eq7" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:first-interactions:eq7">[tra:first-interactions:eq7]</a>, averaged over priorities at the other vertices, is $1-t+t\delta_c$. Jensen’s inequality and integrating in $t$ now lower bound the expected term by $$\sum_c p_c \int_0^1 -\log(1-t+t\delta_c)\,dt.\label{tra:first-interactions:eq8}$$ For $\delta_c=0$ the integral is 1. For all $0\le s\le1$, the integral with $\delta_c=s$ is nonnegative and at least $1-C\sqrt s$: the loss from 1 in the interior is $s\log(1/s)/(1-s)$.

<span id="tra:first-interactions:parallelism-and-heavy-atom-losses" label="tra:first-interactions:parallelism-and-heavy-atom-losses"></span> Call an edge heavy in parallelism if its endpoints have edge multiplicity greater than $a^{1/2}$. We may discard <a href="#tra:first-interactions:eq8" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:first-interactions:eq8">[tra:first-interactions:eq8]</a> for these edges. On another edge $\sum_c\delta_c\le a^{1/2}$. For the colors with $p_c\le a^{-.7}$, we have $$\sum_{c:p_c\le a^{-.7}} p_c\sqrt{\delta_c}
                  \ \le\ \Big(\sum_{c:p_c\le a^{-.7}} p_c\delta_c\Big)^{1/2}
                  \ \le\ a^{-.1}.$$ For the other colors we allow a loss up to their total $p_c$-mass instead in <a href="#tra:first-interactions:eq8" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:first-interactions:eq8">[tra:first-interactions:eq8]</a>. Consequently, summed over edges and averaged, <a href="#tra:first-interactions:eq8" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:first-interactions:eq8">[tra:first-interactions:eq8]</a> bounds $L_{\rm corr}$ below by $n$, less the expected number of edges heavy in parallelism, the sum of the exceptional masses with $p_c>a^{-.7}$ (averaged), and $C n a^{-.1}$.

<a id="tra:first-interactions:eq9"></a>
<a id="tra:first-interactions:eq10"></a>
We check the sizes of these losses using the marginal divergences above. We use the elementary estimate $$D(P\Vert Q)\ \ge\ s P(F)-\log(1+Q(F)(e^s-1))\label{tra:first-interactions:eq9}$$ for $s>0$ and an event $F$, by the entropy inequality (or just projecting to $F$). For $h_v$ given $j$, in the chain of exposing entries use as reference a uniform permutation. Except at most $\lceil a^{.9}\rceil$ late entries per column, it has at least $a^{.9}$ remaining possibilities. The uniform conditional chance to hit the exceptional set for the current $p$ is then at most $a^{-.2}$ (there are at most $a^{.7}$ such colors). Use <a href="#tra:first-interactions:eq9" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:first-interactions:eq9">[tra:first-interactions:eq9]</a> with $s=.09\log a$ at these exposures, with the set fixed conditional on earlier entries and $j$. The relative entropies sum by the chain rule. This bounds the total expected exceptional mass over the edges, including the late-entry loss, by $$C\big((L_h+z_h)/\log a+n a^{-.1}\big).\label{tra:first-interactions:eq10}$$

<a id="tra:first-interactions:eq11"></a>
For parallelism, consider the new marginal law of $j$ against the reference of independent uniform permutations. Expose $j$ by rows (all of one row permutation, then the next) and within each by successive entries. For an entry corresponding to left vertex $u$, count a hit if the target vertex has occurred as target from $u$ already at least $a^{.4}$ times before the entry. There are at most $a^{.6}$ possible hit targets given the earlier entries. At least half the edges heavy in parallelism give hits (in the sense that their endpoint pairs with multiplicity above $a^{1/2}$ give hits on at least half those occurrences, for large $a$). Again discount at most $\lceil b^{.9}\rceil$ late exposures per permutation where the number of possibilities under uniform may be small. Otherwise the uniform conditional chance of a hit is at most $C b^{-.3}$, since $a,b$ are comparable. Applying <a href="#tra:first-interactions:eq9" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:first-interactions:eq9">[tra:first-interactions:eq9]</a> with $s=.09\log b$ as before, the expected number of edges heavy in parallelism is at most $$C\big((L_j+z_j)/\log b+n b^{-.1}\big).\label{tra:first-interactions:eq11}$$ This bounds the loss even if $j$ acquires strong correlations upon conditioning.

The lower bound from <a href="#tra:first-interactions:eq8" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:first-interactions:eq8">[tra:first-interactions:eq8]</a>, with <a href="#tra:first-interactions:eq10" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:first-interactions:eq10">[tra:first-interactions:eq10]</a> and <a href="#tra:first-interactions:eq11" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:first-interactions:eq11">[tra:first-interactions:eq11]</a>, gives $$L_{\rm corr}\ge n-C n^{.98}
                                   - C\,(L_h+L_j+z)/\log n$$ where we use comparability and have loosened the numerical power. In $L$, the losses involving $L_h,L_j$ are paid for by those terms themselves. Thus for sufficiently large $n$ this proves <a href="#tra:first-interactions:eq6" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:first-interactions:eq6">[tra:first-interactions:eq6]</a>. ◻

</details>

<a id="tra:first-interactions:subgroup-product-setup"></a>
#### Crossing projections and dyadic singular bands

Here is how we use the rectangle estimate. By splitting the bit list into segments of lengths $\lfloor d/2\rfloor,\lceil d/2\rceil$, the sweep product takes the form $$A B ,$$ where $A,B$ are group-algebra operators on $H,J_0$, respectively. The roles of rows and columns may be named to have this form. Each operator on its own subgroup is a tensor product (law of independent sweeps) on the separate columns or rows, with the corresponding smaller sizes $a,b$. All estimates below are unchanged if using adjoint operators consistently.

<a id="stmt-tra-first-interactions-projection-fourth-moment"></a>
<div id="tra:first-interactions:projection-fourth-moment" class="lemma">

**Lemma 53**. *<span id="tra:first-interactions:crossing" label="tra:first-interactions:crossing"></span>*

<a id="tra:first-interactions:eq12"></a>
*For orthogonal projections $P,Q$ in the subgroup algebras of $H,J_0$, suppose each is a tensor product over that subgroup’s factors. Let their regular ranks, meaning their ranks in the regular representation of the respective subgroup, be $r_H,r_J$, assumed nonzero. Put $z=\log(r_H r_J)$. We claim that on any irreducible $\lambda$ of $G$, $$D_\lambda \| (P Q)(\lambda) \|_4^4
                 \ \le\ \exp\big(C n^{.98}+(1+C/\log n)z\big),\label{tra:first-interactions:eq12}$$ where $\|\cdot\|_4$ is Schatten 4-norm.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-tra-first-interactions-projection-fourth-moment"><summary>Proof of stmt-tra-first-interactions-projection-fourth-moment</summary>

<a id="tra:first-interactions:eq13"></a>
*Proof.* <span id="tra:first-interactions:regular-coefficient-proof" label="tra:first-interactions:regular-coefficient-proof"></span> It suffices to bound the full regular trace of $PQPQ$, since its irreducible contributions are nonnegative fourth powers with regular multiplicity. Lemma <a href="#lem:coefficient-compatibility" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:coefficient-compatibility">14</a>, applied to the local projections, gives $$\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}_{\rm reg}(PQPQ)
 \le\frac{|G|}{|H||J_0|}\,r_Hr_J\,
       \Pr\{hj\in J_0H\}.
 \label{tra:first-interactions:eq13}$$ Here the line permutations are independent under their normalized squared-coefficient laws, each with density bounded by its local regular rank. These ranks multiply to $r_Hr_J=e^z$, so <a href="#tra:first-interactions:eq6" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:first-interactions:eq6">[tra:first-interactions:eq6]</a> applies with exactly the chosen $z$. Finally $$\frac{|G|}{|H|\,|J_0|}
                    =\frac{n!}{(a!)^b (b!)^a}
                    \ \le\ \exp(n+C\sqrt n\log n)$$ by Stirling’s formula. Combining in <a href="#tra:first-interactions:eq13" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:first-interactions:eq13">[tra:first-interactions:eq13]</a> proves <a href="#tra:first-interactions:eq12" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:first-interactions:eq12">[tra:first-interactions:eq12]</a>, allowing adjustment of the constant in $C n^{.98}$. The main exponential here is why we used the coloring estimate in addition to ranks. ◻

</details>

<details id="proof-stmt-tra-first-interactions-projection-fourth-moment-2"><summary>Proof of stmt-tra-first-interactions-projection-fourth-moment</summary>

*Proof of Theorem <a href="#tra:first-interactions:singular" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="tra:first-interactions:singular">[tra:first-interactions:singular]</a>.* <span id="tra:first-interactions:alt-and-dyadic-band-decay" label="tra:first-interactions:alt-and-dyadic-band-decay"></span> We perform the singular-value induction. The preceding fourth-moment estimate has an error independent of the eventual Schatten exponent. We retain that property while summing the spectral bands; it lets the induction begin from any sufficiently large finite exponent without changing the cutoff in $n$. Suppose for the two smaller sizes the bound in <a href="#tra:first-interactions:eq1" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:first-interactions:eq1">[tra:first-interactions:eq1]</a> holds with $p_0$ (in place of $p_*$), where we can take the larger of the two parameters, always at least 2. We will show how along induction it suffices to increase this parameter by factors at most $1+O(1/\log n)$ for all sufficiently large sizes.

<a id="tra:first-interactions:eq14"></a>
Take $$p=p_0(1+C_0/\log n)$$ with $C_0$ large enough, absolute. For each $\lambda$, we will bound a Schatten trace of $A B$ on the irreducible. Write $X=A^* A$, $Y=B B^*$. Lemma <a href="#lem:positive-power-comparison" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:positive-power-comparison">9</a>, applied on the irreducible block with $A_2=A$, $A_1=B$, $P=2p$ and $q=4$, gives $$\operatorname{Tr}|A B|^{2p}
                      \ \le\ \| X^{p/4} Y^{p/4}\|_4^4 .\label{tra:first-interactions:eq14}$$

<a id="tra:first-interactions:eq15"></a>
Decompose in the subgroup algebras to bound the right side. For $X$, on each of the $b$ column factors take the irreducible matrix-block decomposition and, within each irreducible, the eigenbasis of the corresponding factor of $X$, in order of decreasing eigenvalue. Group indices within this matrix-block into dyadic intervals $[R,2R)$ truncated at its dimension (here $R=1,2,4,\ldots$). Each such interval gives a projection in that factor group algebra of regular rank $$m \cdot (\text{length of interval}),$$ where $m$ is the dimension of this smaller irreducible. Taking tensor products gives projections $P$ as in <a href="#tra:first-interactions:eq12" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:first-interactions:eq12">[tra:first-interactions:eq12]</a> for $H$ that sum to identity. By the smaller-size hypothesis, for each such choice $$\|P X^{p/4}\|_{\rm op}
                                   \le r_H^{-p/(4p_0)},\label{tra:first-interactions:eq15}$$ where the norm bound holds also after lifting to $G$. Indeed squared singular values from an interval on a factor are at most $(m R)^{-1/p_0}$; the interval length is at most $R$. The analogous decomposition of $Y$ over row factors gives $Q$ with $\|Q Y^{p/4}\|_{\rm op}\le r_J^{-p/(4p_0)}$.

<a id="tra:first-interactions:eq16"></a>
<span id="tra:first-interactions:band-count-and-intermediate-trace" label="tra:first-interactions:band-count-and-intermediate-trace"></span> The total number of pairs $P,Q$ in these decompositions is at most $$\exp(C n^{.8}).\label{tra:first-interactions:eq16}$$ In fact per factor of size $a$ or $b$, the number of partitions for its irreducibles is at most $\exp(C\sqrt a)$ or $\exp(C\sqrt b)$, and the number of dyadic intervals in each is at most polynomial in the factor size since dimensions are at most the factorial. The partition bound here is the standard elementary one; for example it follows by using $s=1/\sqrt a$ and bounding the partition generating function at $e^{-s}$ by $\exp(C/s)$, using its product formula (and likewise with $b$).

<a id="tra:first-interactions:eq17"></a>
Use the triangle inequality for Schatten 4-norm to sum terms on the right of <a href="#tra:first-interactions:eq14" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:first-interactions:eq14">[tra:first-interactions:eq14]</a>, inserting these projections. For each $P,Q$, by <a href="#tra:first-interactions:eq12" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:first-interactions:eq12">[tra:first-interactions:eq12]</a>, <a href="#tra:first-interactions:eq15" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:first-interactions:eq15">[tra:first-interactions:eq15]</a> and the ideal property of Schatten norm, we have, on $\lambda$, $$\begin{aligned}
 D_\lambda \| X^{p/4} P Q Y^{p/4} \|_4^4
   &\le \exp\big(- (p/p_0)z + C n^{.98}+(1+C/\log n)z\big)\\
   &\le \exp(C n^{.98}),
 \end{aligned}$$ with our choice of $C_0$. Now summing by <a href="#tra:first-interactions:eq16" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:first-interactions:eq16">[tra:first-interactions:eq16]</a> (triangle inequality before taking fourth powers) still gives by <a href="#tra:first-interactions:eq14" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:first-interactions:eq14">[tra:first-interactions:eq14]</a> $$D_\lambda \operatorname{Tr}|T_n(\lambda)|^{2p}
                                  \le \exp(C_1 n^{.98}),\label{tra:first-interactions:eq17}$$ where $C_1$ is absolute. The placement of the Schatten powers in this proof means we do not have a loss from summing norm bounds raised later to a possibly very large $p$.

<a id="tra:first-interactions:eq18"></a>
<a id="tra:first-interactions:eq19"></a>
<span id="tra:first-interactions:dimension-and-all-index-closure" label="tra:first-interactions:dimension-and-all-index-closure"></span> To use <a href="#tra:first-interactions:eq17" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:first-interactions:eq17">[tra:first-interactions:eq17]</a> and finish the induction, we record simple dimension bounds. For shapes of height exceeding $n/2$ the singular bound was automatic. For the rest with $k=n-\lambda_1\ge n^{.99}$, we have $$\log D_\lambda\ge c n^{.99}\label{tra:first-interactions:eq18}$$ for large $n$, with an absolute $c>0$. Here and later we can see this type of lower bound as follows. Transpose a partition if needed and let $u$ be its first row length after taking the larger of width and height. If $u<n/8$, the hook lengths are at most $2u$, so the dimension is at least $(n/(2eu))^n$ by the hook formula. For $u\ge n/8$, put $t=n-u$. The hook formula gives at least $$\binom{n}{t}\exp\left(-C\frac{t}{u}\log(u+1)\right),\label{tra:first-interactions:eq19}$$ since we may drop the dimension (a factor at least 1) of the partition below that row, and the correction to row factorial uses log factors $\log(1+c_j/(u-j+1))$, where $c_j$ counts cells below in column $j$. Indeed $jc_j\le t$, and $$\sum_{j=1}^{u}\log\left(1+\frac{c_j}{u-j+1}\right)
 \le t\sum_{j=1}^{u}\frac{1}{j(u-j+1)}
 =\frac{2t}{u+1}\sum_{j=1}^{u}\frac1j.$$ This proves the displayed correction, including the range in which the tail is not small. For $n/8\le u\le n/2$, <a href="#tra:first-interactions:eq19" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:first-interactions:eq19">[tra:first-interactions:eq19]</a> gives log dimension of order at least $c' n$. For $u>n/2$ under our height restriction before transposition, $u=\lambda_1$, so $t=k$; <a href="#tra:first-interactions:eq18" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:first-interactions:eq18">[tra:first-interactions:eq18]</a> follows using <a href="#tra:first-interactions:eq19" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:first-interactions:eq19">[tra:first-interactions:eq19]</a> and $\binom{n}{t}\ge (n/t)^t$.

Hence in this dense case <a href="#tra:first-interactions:eq17" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tra:first-interactions:eq17">[tra:first-interactions:eq17]</a> yields $$\begin{aligned}
